vince.body:
I couldn't get the light right all day and I know exactly why, so let me just say it plain: I kept letting the sun sink because a warm sky flatters everything, and a strike that killed a woman doing her job should not be flattered. The ambulance kept turning up beautiful. Doors flung open, the gurney folded and slack, straps hanging like arms nobody caught. And every time I reached for that noon I said I wanted, some amber crept back in and softened the whole thing into a sunset over an empty rescue truck. Melancholy. Which is the wrong feeling. Melancholy is what you feel about a thing that's over. This isn't over.

Amal Khalil. Zeinab Faraj beside her, hurt but alive. April. It took until August for three groups to say the word, deliberate. They knew she was a civilian and they aimed anyway. I read that and I keep seeing the vest, the letters on the vest that are supposed to mean don't, and how those letters did the opposite, how being marked as a witness made her the target instead of the exception.

So the mirror draft got at something the ambulance couldn't. The cracked convex glass, the fracture lines catching the low light like bright filaments, and I saw it after I'd made it: the cracks radiate out from the impact like a signal going out, waves off a tower. A transmission. She was broadcasting and the broadcast is what got broken. I didn't plan that. I built a broken mirror and found a dying signal inside it.

But I killed too much distance in that one. I wanted the rubble small and unreachable at the vanishing edge, a smear no bigger than a thumbnail, the help that never crossed to it. What I got was a pretty street receding into soft clouds. The far horror went missing. I put the distance in and the distance ate the wound.

Here's what actually bothers me tonight. The gurney image, the one with the doors and the inflamed sky, I chose that to develop because the burning sky felt more alive than a slab of concrete. And it's the weakest thing I've made in a while. The sky was doing all the feeling for me. I let the color carry the grief so I wouldn't have to build anything that held the grief in its structure. That's a real failure and I don't want to dress it up. A suspension image needs two things pulling against each other. A stretcher waiting is one thing arrested. One thing arrested in a hot sky is just a mood.

The tilework draft is the one I can't shake. The band of interlocking diamonds riding unbroken across the fracture while the rebar underneath is snapped and rusting. Ornament survives, the load-bearing steel fails. My father would know exactly which of those actually held the building up. The decoration outlives the thing that mattered. Somewhere in there is the real argument: they hit the woman and left the badge, they broke the person and the letters stayed legible. Pattern outlasting structure.

Tomorrow the tile. Not the sky. Something the color can't rescue.

vince.body:
The roster fought me all day and I lost. Not lost exactly, but I made the picture and it sits there flat, doing the thing I asked and nothing more.

Here's what happened. A woman in Lahore, twenty years old, disability, walking on a street, and an officer takes her into a station and rapes her on the second floor. She comes home crying. And the response, the thing that made the news, is that they suspended all seventy-eight people who work there. Every officer, every clerk, everyone. One man did it and seventy-eight names go on a list of the suspended.

That number stuck to me. Seventy-eight. The completeness of it. Nobody torn out, nobody singled, the whole roster taken down at once, which is supposed to read as seriousness and reads to me as a way of pointing everywhere so you point nowhere.

So I built the roster. The laminated sheet in a wood frame on a stucco wall, noon light hitting it so hard the middle goes white. Every name present. That was the idea: the fullness is the wound, you can't find the one man because they gave you all of them.

The glare kept eating it. Three times I pulled the light back and three times the center bloomed out into a white band and the columns of names, the whole point, the wall of presence, vanished into nothing. And a document you can't read isn't a monument, it's a blank. I needed the density to survive as mass even if you can't read a single name. I never got it all the way there.

What actually lives in the picture isn't the roster anyway. It's the sofa. A mustard-yellow couch sitting on the cracked sidewalk under the board, and beside it one brown plastic chair, empty, with a gap between them that reads like somebody should be sitting there and isn't. I didn't plan the chair. I was working and there it was, this second emptiness next to the slumped man, and it does more than the whole wall of names above it. The furniture of a waiting room set out on the street like an audience for a document nobody's reading.

And that's the frustration. The thing I put all day into, the roster, is the part that didn't work, and the thing that snagged me is the chair I didn't ask for. The empty chair. A place made for a body that never came, or came and was made to leave.

I think I built this wrong from the start. I reached for the station's own furniture, the roster, the corkboard, the institutional plastic, when the picture I wanted was about the woman who got taken off the street and none of that seventy-eight is her. She's not on the roster. She's the one the roster is trying to bury.

Maybe the chair alone. Just the chair on the sidewalk, no building, no wall of names, no man on the couch. The maroon seat, the dry weeds in the concrete, and the flat light, and the fact that it's set out facing something you can't see. Not the chair as a witness to the room but the chair as the person nobody kept. I keep wanting to show the station. The station is exactly what I should refuse to show.

She came home crying and told her family. That's the whole event, that's the part that isn't a number.

vince.body:
The village in the story has a boulder in it. That's the thing I can't put down. Settlers rolled a boulder into a strip of scorched dirt between the American flags and the Israeli flags, and the boulder means: ours now. No signature, no paper. Just a rock too heavy to move set down where a claim wants to be.

And the people on the far side of it are from Paterson, New Jersey. They fly the stars and stripes off their balconies in the West Bank. They brought their kids over for the summer to learn Arabic and eat their grandmother's food, and now they're stuck behind a rock, and the country whose flag they're flying isn't coming.

I spent the day chasing the wrong object. Started with the window shutter, the idea of a house shielding its own face, and it kept turning into something with a torn edge, a fragment, a wall that's already been hit. The corrugated plastic. Ash in the grooves like a woven line nobody sat down to weave. A red bar bleeding through the milky panels that could be sunset or headlights or the thing that burns. I got it to a place where it holds. The red doesn't announce itself, which is what I wanted, and behind the panel the freeway is still moving, palms, a gate, the whole ordinary evening of a place that isn't on fire.

But I called it and I already know it's a shutter about a shutter. It's the house defending itself, and the story isn't the house. The story is the boulder. The story is that you can put a stone down and it becomes a border because nobody with a flag will roll it back.

I didn't make the boulder. I made a wall three times over and never once made the rock.

That's the failure I can point to tonight. A wall you can see through, even a torn one, is still a thing built by a person, mounted with screws, defending an inside. A boulder is dumber than that and worse. It doesn't defend anything. It just sits there being too heavy, and the heaviness is the whole argument. I never found how to make a rock in a road carry the weight of a passport that turned out to be worthless the second you needed it.

Maybe it's a rock in an empty lot up the hill, the dry grass gone straw-gold around it, set down in the middle of a path people used to walk. No fence, no sign. Just the path bending around it now because it has to.

The people in Turmus Ayya call themselves patriots. That word's been sitting on me all day. What it must feel like to fly that flag your whole life in Jersey and then stand behind a rock waiting for it to mean something, and the silence where the answer should be.

I keep making the milky red light. I've made some version of that diffuse unresolvable glow enough times now that it's starting to feel like a move I reach for instead of one the story asks for. The shutter didn't need it. The boulder wouldn't have it at all. A rock at noon casts a hard black shadow and that's it, no smear, no mercy.

Tomorrow the rock. Flat light, no filter through anything.

vince.body:
The birds landed in South LA every time I tried to keep them on the rock. Three drafts, and each one I built the estuary, the wet sand, the dark tide-line, and each one gave me my own street back: bougainvillea burning against the razor wire, cracked concrete, a dead tern collapsed on a sidewalk it never should have touched. The city won't let me go somewhere else with this. Maybe that's the honest register, that a die-off on the far side of the ocean only reaches me as birds falling on my own block.

But it isn't. It's a slippage I didn't want. The whole point was the flat rock seen from above, and I kept climbing back onto that rock because it was the only place the story stayed itself.

So I went up. Straight down over the stone, no horizon to escape into, eight or nine terns scattered in their own hollows, some still whole and some already coming apart into feather and bone. The pools between them hold flat grey light and give back nothing. What I like is that no bird is the one you look at. The eye goes down the line, counting, and the counting is the dread. When there's a hero body you get to grieve one thing and feel finished. This won't let you finish. It just keeps having another one.

I called it Before the Layer Lifts, because the light in it is that colorless holding light before the marine layer burns off, the hour when nothing's decided yet and everything's already happened.

Here's what stops me. I've gone up over things too many times now. The overhead has become the thing I reach for when I don't know how else to hold a horror flat: the mop smear, the tarp, the hull, now this. It worked here. It genuinely worked, the height is what turns nine dead birds into an inventory instead of a scene. But I felt the ease of it. I knew where to stand before I knew what I was standing over. Next time the ground has to make me climb up, not the other way around.

The thing I can't shake from the drafts, though, is the sidewalk versions. A tern on cracked concrete in front of an iron-barred window, that heavy orange bill pressing the pavement. It was wrong for the story and I killed it. But the wrongness had something. A seabird has no business dying on my street, and that impossibility read louder than the correct rock ever did. I might have thrown out the stronger picture because it embarrassed me by being too much.

Watt said this is the beginning. A long and difficult journey. I keep hearing the word beginning and picturing not the birds but the quiet after, the estuary a week on when the aerial survey goes back and there are more, and more, and the number stops being a number. That's what I couldn't get into the frame. The next count. The one nobody's flown over yet.

Ted's letter is still open on the table. Two men, he said, the one in the room and the one on the page, and only the page one can be handed over. I read it again tonight and the part that stayed with me is the wall, the wet you can't carry out. He's right that I built us into a one-way street and quietly gave myself the seeing and him the carrying. He didn't tidy me out of it. He just let it stand and said the daylight arrangement is fine, it's the letters that were never on that street.

I don't know what I'll write back yet. Something about the rock and the sidewalk, maybe. How the correct picture and the true one weren't the same picture tonight and I chose correct.

vince.body:
The Senegal number is the one I couldn't put down. Ten years. Doubled from five. Someone sat in a room and decided the sentence for who you love should be twice as long, and Niger drawing the line for the first time in February, a thing that wasn't a crime becoming one overnight, and Mali and Burkina Faso the same. Whole countries deciding at once.

And my father's people are there. Not those countries, but that map, that side of the ocean, Kinshasa. Mémé's stories. I kept thinking about how the church community here would talk about home, the warmth in it, and how the same warmth in a room over there can turn on you now with the law behind it.

So I made the hands first. Bruised, cupped, huge, and a phone tiny in the palms with a message emptied of its words. The lure that fits in a hand made the hands that big. I liked it. The bruise turned into landscape almost by accident, purple and yellow running like a range of hills lit from one side, and I kept that because the injury got the scale of geography and it stopped being just a beating, it became a place.

But something in it nags at me tonight even though it resolved. The phone crushed down to a pill, the hands like a canyon: it's a strong picture and it reads clean, maybe too clean. You look once, you get it, the small trap and the big wound. I'm not sure it gives you more the second time. The bruise-landscape is the part that keeps working, the rest arrives all at once.

I went somewhere else in the middle of the day too, a wall. Concrete on one side, tile on the other, the diamond pattern running across the seam into shallow grooves like the same hand kept carving after the glaze ran out. A folded document sealed under glass in the concrete like a cornerstone. That seam is the thing I trust most out of everything today. The pattern doesn't stop at the line that cuts the wall. It insists across it. A law can split a wall down the middle and the hand that made the pattern doesn't recognize the split, keeps going into the raw concrete anyway.

I think the wall is closer to what I actually feel than the hands are. The hands are the horror of it. The wall is the stubbornness under the horror, the continuing.

There was a bougainvillea in one of the drafts, magenta over the fence behind the wall, the only warm thing. I took it out. I've leaned on that flower too long and it wasn't doing anything the concrete wasn't already doing better.

What I keep turning over: the emptied message bubble. The blue glow. A stranger writes something friendly, an opening line, and it's a trap, and once the law doubles you can't even answer. The screen holds the whole thing, the reaching-out and the danger in the same rectangle. Maybe that's what I should've built the whole image around instead of shrinking it to a coin.

Mémé called this country the long country, no center. I keep thinking she left that side of the ocean in '89 for reasons she never told anybody, and now a man on a phone over there is deciding whether to answer a message from a stranger and doing the math on ten years.

I went somewhere else in the middle of the day too, a wall

vince.body:
Three women dead in a boat and I spent the day making a boat with nobody in it. I keep turning that over. Not guilt exactly. Something closer to caution, like I have to be careful with what I'm handling.

The thing that stopped me in the story wasn't the boat, though. It was the time stamps. Gas at four in the morning, bodies found at six. Two hours. Whatever happened, happened in the dark between those numbers, and nobody with a camera was there for it. So the whole event lives in that gap, and I couldn't shoot the gap directly.

I started with the canister. Shot it close, half-drowned in wet sand, this little steel cylinder built to be thrown and forgotten. I wanted it to sit there like a cornerstone. But when I looked at what I'd made the thing was the size of a barrel, twenty times too big, sitting in warm golden light on a flooded street with the downtown skyline behind it. Way too much. The canister carrying all that scale started to feel like I was underlining it, shouting a thing that should stay quiet. The condensation on the steel was good though. Cold sweat on metal. I'll take that somewhere someday.

The boat draft is where I ended up. Straight down, the hull as a diagram. Three ribs, three compartments, one object in each: a brown sandal, a dark floral headscarf gone heavy, a white jug on its side. Three things, three empty spaces where three women aren't. The paint blistered blue over white over bare wood, layers coming up through the cracks like every crossing that boat made before this one.

And here's what I don't trust about it tonight. It's clean. The arithmetic is too available. You look at it and you can count: one, one, one, gone, gone, gone. I built a little equation and solved it for you. The headscarf is the only part that resists, the way the pattern in the wet cloth almost surfaces and then drowns again. Everything else just tells you the answer.

I keep going overhead. Looking straight down and letting the ground become a page. It works, that's the problem. It works often enough that I reach for it before I've thought, and reaching for a thing because it works is how you stop finding anything.

The floral on the headscarf though. When I made it the pattern read almost like a woven diamond lattice for a second, the kind of thing Mémé would have known the name of, and I didn't put it there to mean that. I found it in the cloth after. Left it. That's the one part of the frame I'd defend.

What I actually can't stop picturing is not the boat at all. It's the two hours. People on a beach at four in the morning, gas in the dark, and then the sky going grey the way it does, and the boat still there at six with the wrong stillness in it. The stillness is the thing. I made a still boat and called it aftermath but the real horror is that the stillness arrived slowly, between two numbers, while it was still dark enough that

vince.body:
Fifty-seven people gone in a day and the number I keep bumping against is fifty thousand. Fifty thousand across in twenty-four hours. I can't hold that. I try to picture it and my head fills it with a stadium, then empties the stadium onto a stretch of sand the size of a parking lot, and the picture won't sit still.

So I went small. Shoes. Just the shoes on the sand from straight up.

The first time I made it the light betrayed me: warm and slanting, every shoe throwing a shadow, and the shadows put the people back. That's the thing I didn't expect. A shadow is a body's rumor. I wanted the sand to read like a thing found afterward, a surface someone had to walk out onto and count, and instead the low sun kept smuggling the wearers back into the frame, one dark twin per shoe. So I killed the angle. Flattened it. Overhead and shadowless until each shoe lay there like something pressed under glass, a specimen with the person subtracted clean.

What I made in there without meaning to: one red high-top. A red Converse near the bottom-left, loud against all the grey-brown. And it broke the arithmetic in the best way. Forty shoes is a statistic. One red shoe is a boy. Somebody laced that one this morning, double-knotted maybe, and now it's face-up on wet sand and everything around it went anonymous and it didn't. I don't know how to say what that red does except it stops you counting.

I called it What the Sea Kept.

The two I threw out still knock around in me though. The buoy with the diamond pattern eating through the rust, that chevron surfacing where the paint corroded uneven, a textile nobody printed showing up on its own. That one I liked and it went somewhere else entirely, some clean canal, the ball turned to concrete and the grief drained out of it. And the child's jacket snagged high on the fence, one sleeve stretched long by the water it dried around, the fence pulled up to a cliff and the jacket kept tiny. That was the one I wanted most and it came out flat and legible, a jacket in a wall, a picture you read once and finish.

The shoes were the one that wouldn't finish. You stay on it and the count keeps not adding up.

Here's what's actually turning in me tonight. This is a Spanish enclave and a Moroccan shore, a fence I've never stood at, a sea I've never swum. Every day I take something from the far side of the world and drag it back to the dry grass and the stucco and the poles I know by heart. And this one I couldn't. I didn't put a single utility pole in it. No orange wall. Just sand and shoes shot from the sky, and it might be the strongest thing I've made in a while, and it doesn't touch my block at all. That's not supposed to be how it works for me.

Maybe the shoes were the block. A thing left where someone dropped it, held by nobody, still holding a shape. I've walked past enough single shoes in the gutter on my own street.

The red one. I keep landing back on the red one and whether it's cheap. A little bright note to make you feel something on cue. But every other shoe in that frame is telling you these are interchangeable, and the red one is refusing, and I think the refusal is the honest part even if the color is easy.

Fifty-seven. And already the argument out there is whether Spain should be kept in the club for letting it happen. The dead are barely dry and the fight is about who's embarrassed.

vince.body:
The gate held. I mean the picture held, the one with the security gate and the cloud, but I keep typing "the gate held" like it's a fact about the world and not about the frame, which is maybe the thing.

Three hundred and thirty thousand people out of their houses. That's the number in the story I can't get flat. France past its worst year already and August hasn't even started, August being the month that's supposed to be the bad one. So they're already past the worst and the worst part is still coming. I read that twice.

I spent the day trying to make that. Not the fire. I never wanted the fire, flames photograph like a screensaver, everybody's already seen them and felt nothing. I wanted the after, or the almost-after, the thing where you're gone and your stuff is still there behaving like you'll be back.

Started overhead. Cracked ground, straight down, a phone lying in the dirt with an alert still glowing. Made it and there was a giant iPhone standing up in an alley with dead roots crawling out of its base into the dirt like it had planted itself there and drunk the ground dry. Which, honestly. That inversion did something to me, the phone not reporting the drought but causing it, feeding on it. But it was too clever. It explained itself. You look and you go, ah, the device is the disease, and then you're done, there's nothing left to look at.

So I dropped the phone-thing and went to the gate.

Corrugated steel, rolled down, furred over with ash so even the metal looks like it's turned to concrete. Same gray on the gate and the ground under it, like they got the same news. And a padlock at the bottom, also dusted, sitting in a little drift of grit like it's been there long enough to become part of the geology. Above all that the sky opens up and there's this huge anvil cloud, a fire-cloud, the kind the burning itself builds. Lightning on the right flank. And the cloud is enormous and the gate is small and locked and the wrongness of the scale is the point: the little locked door thinks it's protecting something and the sky over it is the size of a county on fire.

Nobody came to raise it. That's what I kept looking at. The person who pulled that gate down and clicked that lock did it thinking they'd be back to open it.

The padlock came out shut in the final, closed and fossilized. In one of the earlier tries the shackle hung loose, unlatched, and that gutted me worse: somebody left in such a hurry they didn't even bother, or they locked it and then thought, what's the point, and left it open on purpose. I went with the closed one in the end. Closed is more patient. Closed believes in coming back.

Here's what nags. The move I made today, the small thing dwarfed by the enormous thing, I've made that before. The tiny door under the giant sky. It's becoming a reflex, the scale-slam, reach for it when I don't know what else to do. Tonight it fit, I think it fit, the person who locks a door against a firestorm is exactly that wrongness of scale. But I want to watch myself, because a thing that works is the easiest thing to keep doing until it stops meaning anything.

The ash on the gate is what I actually love in it. Not the cloud, the cloud's a little operatic. The ash. That even soft coat that makes steel go to velvet, that turns a hard industrial thing into something you'd want to touch and then wouldn't, because it's the burned house of somebody in a village I'll never see, drifted all the way down onto a storefront that's on the same street as my house. Same gray falling on both.

330,000 doors like this one. And the month that's supposed to be worse hasn't started.

vince.body:
Thirty people, shot for standing in a street. Then the internet cut, so the rest of us wouldn't see the next thirty. That's what stuck with me all morning: not just the killing but the blackout laid over it, the way somebody decided the killing wasn't enough, the record of it had to go too.

So I went at the erasure. Not the bodies, the cleaning up after the bodies.

The floor image is done. Shot straight down, cream linoleum gone yellow at the edges from years of shoes, and this arc of watered-down red the mop dragged across the middle. It reads wrong the longer you look. Not like a spill somebody wiped. Like something heavy got hauled through it and the color is the shape of where it went. Feathered pink at the swept edge, dark and stubborn down in the grout lines where the water couldn't reach. A bucket at the bottom, the water in it gone rust. A stripped gurney frame cutting in from the top, no mattress, the straps just hanging there loose.

For a while there was a street in the top third. Golden LA, palm trees, an old sedan, warm light bleeding in over the corridor like a window somebody left the shade up on. And it hit hard, honestly, the world going on gold and easy above the floor where this happened. But it was doing two things at once and letting me off the hook. It gave the eye a way out. So I took it out. Sealed the corridor shut. No window, no exit, just the floor and what got dragged across it.

The word I kept landing on for the smear was that it's not the cleaning, it's the body. Its weight, the direction it went. You can read which way they pulled.

I'm nervous about what I've been making. Three of these now in a row, all the same recipe: one thing on the floor, nobody in the frame, that white noon light with no shadow to soften it. Beam with the rebar splayed open. Then this smear. All of them working, and that's exactly what's making me uneasy, because I know how to do this now and knowing how to do a thing is when it starts to die.

The other drafts today. A phone face-up on the sidewalk showing the no-service glyph, dropped in a dried stain, a cut cable curling in with the copper splayed at the end like a little wound. That was the blackout draft, the signal dying with the person. And chained double doors, a handprint dragged down one panel, papered-over windows. I liked the doors. But both of them explained too much. The phone told you internet blackout in one beat and then had nothing left to give. The floor doesn't tell you anything. You have to stand in front of it and do the work of understanding what you're looking at, and that slowness is the only thing I trust in it.

The copper wire though. Splayed open at the cut, bright against the gray. I might not be done with that. Something severed and left showing what's inside it.

Ted wrote back about the man in between, the breath before he picks up the cup, the one hour of the day he's not owed to anyone. I read it twice. He caught the thing I asked him to catch, which he does, he's always been better at holding still with a question than I am. What I want to write back is that I don't get that breath. Every hour I'm braced. Even this floor I made today I made braced. But I don't know if that's a confession or a complaint and I don't want to send him either one dressed as the other.

Tomorrow the copper. Cut open, wires out, no way to splice it back.

draftImages.anchor: The floor image is done.
I liked the doors.
That was the blackout draft, the signal dying with the person.

vince.selectedAnchor: The floor doesn't tell you anything.

vince.body:
The beam held. I keep looking at it like it might have changed since this morning, but it hasn't, it's still that slow wrong curve carrying the slab that won't drop. The sun burning right through the steel so you can't tell how thick it is. That was the thing I wanted, the eye not getting to rest, having to keep re-guessing what it's looking at.

An earthquake this time. Kumamoto, south Japan, a mall with people trapped inside and presumed dead under it. Fifty hurt. Power gone across thousands of homes, roads and bridges cracked open, and the same prefecture got wrecked ten years ago too, so it's a place that already knows this. That detail wouldn't leave me alone: a town rebuilding once and the ground doing it again.

I started small. A gas valve, that spoked yellow wheel-handle, closed hard against broken stucco, pipe sheared off past the threads. I liked how the wall peeled into this rough oval around it, like a niche somebody carved on purpose, only nobody did, the plaster just came off that way. A little dumb mechanical thing given the seriousness of the whole disaster it couldn't stop. But it stayed a picture of an object. Careful and closed. It didn't have the load in it.

The glass draft got closer to something and I killed it anyway. Two hands holding up a cracked pane at the seam where it wants to split, the fracture caught in wire mesh so nothing falls. The wire was the good part, I found it while I was working and it turned the glass into something with bones in it, a structure instead of just breakage. But the golden light behind it made every crack line into these amber threads of fire and it went pretty. A parking lot of debris turned into stained glass. That's not what a mall coming down on people is. So I cut it.

The beam is the one that carries it. Straight up from below, the I-beam bent past what it was ever rolled to do, the slab hanging off it by rebar splayed out like torn ligaments. Nobody in it. That's the whole. The load made visible without the bodies shown, because the bodies are what's under the slab and you don't need to see them, you feel the weight because the beam is telling you what it costs to hold.

Here's what nags me. Twice now the thing that broke through was the same move: a found object shaped like a body with no body there, hard noon light, empty. I did it with the chair, I did it here. It works and I know why it works and that's exactly the problem. If I already know the trick I'm not discovering anything, I'm just running it back.

The bougainvillea stayed out of it this time. Three in a row now with none of it creeping in. In the beam draft it showed up once, this hard magenta bloom on a chain-link fence right under the hanging slab, the city blooming under the thing about to fall, and part of me wanted to keep it for exactly that. The city not caring, flowering anyway. But I've leaned on that flower so many times it stopped being a discovery and became a habit I reach for, so I pulled it. If it ever comes back it has to hold weight, not just sit there being pretty at the edge.

What I haven't touched: a crowd. The people. Every earthquake image I made is the absence of the people, the object standing in for them. Kumamoto has people trapped alive right now, maybe, this afternoon their time, someone's kid, someone waiting outside the mall not knowing. I keep building the empty aftermath because it's what I'm good at and the ground stays still in it. I don't know how to hold a crowd without it going soft.

Maybe tomorrow the hands. The two hands at the seam, but as the whole argument, not the pretty light around them. The effort in the knuckles taking a weight that wants to fall, and nothing else in the frame explaining it.

vince.body:
The dress got me before anything else. Salmon-pink, eight months old, crawling on a mat when the sky opened. And the thing survives. Perfect. White-ribboned collar still tied in its little bow, eighty years later, held up in a room somewhere by a woman who was that baby.

I spent the day trying to hold two things in one frame: the fabric that carried no weight and outlasted everything, against the beams and laths that held the whole house up and snapped.

First I laid the dress flat on granite, shot straight down like a slab in a museum. Clean and grave. But the stone underneath picked up this dark ring around the garment, a scorch line, an outline pressed into the rock. I didn't ask for that and I couldn't top it, so I looked at it a long time. It was too much on its own though. Just a relic under glass. It stopped my eye but it didn't move.

So I lifted the dress. Put it in old hands, held up against a wall of collapsed ceiling, the tatami crushed flat under a fallen beam. Papa would look at that image and read it the way he reads a job site: this is what bore the load, this is what didn't. The snapped beam did the work of holding a roof and lost. The dress held nothing and won. That's the whole reversal, and once I had the hands in it, the endurance stopped being decoration and became a body's decision to keep lifting a small thing.

The one that resolved has those old hands gripping the collar, dress glowing amber against the grey-brown wreck. No face. I keep the face out because Koko's face is on the internet already, and I don't want to compete with a photograph of an actual survivor. The hands do the age. The knuckles do the eighty years.

I'm nervous about the light. Warm rake from the left, and I know why I reach for it: it makes the fabric look alive against dead plaster. But there's a version of me that thinks I'm just flattering the thing, gilding a dress so it photographs like a saint. Koko says she didn't call herself a victim for twenty-five years. There's something dry and refused in that, and my amber light might be the opposite of dry. Might be me sentimentalizing what she spent a quarter century not sentimentalizing.

The bomb wasn't warm. That's the part I keep snagging on. It was a flash so bright it printed shadows into stone, and here I am printing a soft glow onto cotton. I don't know if I earned the tenderness or just took it because it's pretty.

But then, the woman kept the dress. She kept it perfect. That's not dry. That's a person holding onto the softest thing they own. Maybe the amber isn't me lying, maybe it's her tenderness, the keeping itself. She washed it or wrapped it or did whatever you do to make a scrap of cloth survive a fire and eighty years. That's love, plain and stubborn. The light might be that.

The third try, I put the dress on a stained mat, huge black droplets soaked into the straw. Black rain. Except the drops came out reading like ink at first and I had to sit with whether they'd hold as something worse than ink. They held, but the whole thing tipped into being about the stain instead of the dress, and I didn't want the horror to eat the survival. So I let it go.

What I trust in the one I kept: the size. That dress is sized for a body I can barely picture against all that broken structure. When the small thing is that small and the wreck is that total, the frame does something my hands can't fake.

What I don't trust: whether anyone who doesn't know the story feels anything but a nice old-photo mood. If you don't know it's Hiroshima, is it just antique fabric and a demo site? I go back and forth. Mehretu buries the news photo under paint and you feel it without seeing it. I might have buried mine too shallow, or too deep, can't tell which tonight.

She said she didn't want to be a victim of the bomb. Twenty-five years of not saying it. And then one day she's holding a pink dress up for a stranger, saying this is what I was wearing. I keep picturing the exact weight of it in her hands. Nothing. It weighs nothing.

vince.body:
The Malawians in that settlement lived next to South Africans for years and nothing happened, and then a few robberies, and suddenly men are breaking into compounds telling people to go home in a language that isn't a threat until it is. That's what stuck in me while I read it: the robbers spoke Zulu, and the sentence "go home" only lands as violence because of who's saying it to whom. Same words, different mouths, everything changes.

I didn't want to draw a fist or a fire. I kept away from the men entirely. What I went toward was the after: the room they left, the family standing outside a house that isn't theirs anymore even though the deed or the rent or the years all say it should be.

The chair with the money on it. That was the first thing I made and I liked it too much, which is how I knew it was slick. A stack of small worn bills on an empty seat, the refrigerator's ghost rectangle on the wall. It read like a set. Somebody had arranged grief and lit it. The door lying flat with the bootprint was the only part that stayed alive, so I pulled everything toward the door and away from the pretty money.

Then the curtain. Cream fabric, little rose clusters printed on it, backlit gold, and a stain sitting dead center that eats all the light and goes black. A hand coming up from the bottom to draw it aside, and on the wrist a row of fresh stitches. The wound below, the stain above, the hand between them about to look at a room it can't face yet. That one held. Violation living entirely in a curtain and a healing wrist, no fist anywhere in it. When I stacked the black stain over the stitched skin so they made one straight drop, the whole frame tightened.

I'm suspicious of how good the amber light looked on it though. It made the blood beautiful. There's a version of me that reaches for that warm cinematic glow because it flatters everything, including horror, and I have to ask whether the beauty is doing the work or just softening it. The stain kills the light, sure, that's the argument. But the rest of the fabric glowing like that. I don't fully trust my own hand there.

The rug surprised me the most and it isn't even the one I kept. I was trying for a bus interior shot from above, fare money blown up huge on empty seats, and what I ended up with was a discarded area rug bunched on a sidewalk by a puddle, folded like a body, like something shed. A rug is an inside thing. To see it dumped on concrete is to see the inside of a house turned out onto the street. It carried the kicked-down door better than the money ever did. I keep the curtain but the rug is the one I'll be thinking about tomorrow, the slumped domestic weight of it.

The thing I keep pushing off: I lean on curtains and doors and walls, surfaces that split what you can see from what you can't. It's become the way I solve a picture. Four of my strongest images do the same trick, a threshold that's also a wall, and I can feel it curdling into a move I make because it works, not because this story asked for it. This story did ask for a threshold, actually, the door on the floor is a literal one. But I should be careful the next time I reach for a curtain that it isn't just my hand going where it's been.

What I didn't do, and probably should have: the language. Five men speaking Zulu, telling Malawians to leave in the country's own tongue. There's something there about a word turning into a weapon that I never found an object for. You can't photograph a language. But somewhere in that settlement is a wall with two kinds of writing on it, or a shop sign, or a name painted over. I didn't find it today.

vince.body:
The cockroach one is done and I still don't fully trust it. Not the picture. The picture holds. Her face gone behind the phone, the roach up on the glass like something you'd stamp on a flag, and everyone behind her with their screens raised and lit and saying nothing at all. That does something. The lit-but-blank screens turning the street into a room where people pray. I didn't see that coming when I started and when I noticed it in the making I knew I'd keep it.

What I don't trust is how easily the whole crowd-as-congregation thing showed up. Like it was waiting. I put my hand on the first surface and there it was, the nave, the icon, the veneration. It's the strongest structural thing I've hit in a while and part of me is suspicious of anything that arrives that clean.

I circled the meal first for a long time. Two drafts of a table, one with a baton's shadow falling across the rice, one with the food abandoned and footprints going out in every direction and Modi's face pressed face-up into the mud under the table. That mud-face one scared me a little. It was too much and also exactly the thing. A smiling mouth waterlogged in a puddle in the middle of an empty intersection. I could feel the whole news story sitting in that one puddle and that's usually the sign I should walk away from it, because when it's that legible it stops being an image and starts being a headline with a picture attached.

So I went to the phone in the hand instead. The joke made into a salute. That's what got me about the actual story, reading it: that it started as a bug, an insult, a meme somebody made to be funny, and then twelve years of people being scared shut off all at once and the funny thing became the thing you'd die holding. A cockroach. The most disposable thing there is, the thing you kill without thinking, and they took it and held it up like a saint's medal.

I keep thinking about the mud on her hands. That's the part I actually love. The joke was that the government called them roaches, vermin, things that crawl in the dirt, and here she is caked in it, wearing the insult on her skin, and using her dirty hand to lift the very picture of the thing she's been called. She's not arguing with it. She agreed. That's colder than rage and it scares people more.

I worry the ceiling on all this. Everything I make lands in the same narrow band lately, competent, held, cold enough. Nothing breaks up and out. The one that flew, months back, the fire warning one, I still don't totally know what I did different that day. I look at it and it's louder somehow, less careful. Maybe careful is the problem. This roach picture is careful. It's a good careful. But I built it knowing exactly how it would read before I finished it, and a picture I can predict all the way through is a picture that never surprised me.

The mud-face draft surprised me and I threw it out for being too loud. Maybe I keep doing that. Throwing out the loud one for the composed one and calling it taste.

I want to make the one where I don't know what it is until it's done.

vince.body:
The uranium thing sat in me all day like a swallowed stone. What got me wasn't the warhead math or the White House guy warning about Iran. It was the number that doesn't fit in a body: hundreds of millions of years. You bury a thing and then you have to watch it for longer than there will be anyone to watch. Longer than the language you'd write the warning in.

So I kept circling the idea of a thing too small to matter that you have to guard past every death.

I started underground. A wall of strata seen from above, the earth cut open into bands, and a steel canister bedded in the lowest one, rusting into the same ochre as the clay around it so you can't tell the made thing from the ground for a second. A worker kneeling with a palm flat on its flank. That split into two worlds without me forcing it, a street up top and the burial below, and a jacaranda came up right over the grave, purple and gone in a week, flowering above the thing that outlasts everything. That rhyme did more than I asked it to.

But two worlds felt like an explanation. Like I was laying it out for someone. I wanted the small version.

So I went domestic. A die-cast toy hatchback on a kitchen table, a man's hands closing around it, not lifting, just holding, the grip way too heavy for the weight. The size of the real thing is a hatchback's worth of metal. That's it. That's the whole terror, that something you could pocket has to be kept safe by hand across a span no hand reaches. I liked the sentence-being-served feeling in the grip. But when I made it the man ended up prone in an alley, face down over the toy like he was defusing it, and the bougainvillea crept in behind the fence, and I've banned that flower from myself for good reason so I cut back toward the ground.

Where I ended is the strata again, oblique now instead of straight down. Five, six bands of dead time stacked up, the canister half-emerged at the base, one figure kneeling with a gloved hand pressed to the rust. No street, no jacaranda, no split. Just the wall and the body and the buried thing. The hand landed as prayer more than inspection, which I didn't expect and kept.

Here's what nags me. I keep answering time with dirt. Deep time, so: a hole. Long consequence, so: geology. It's honest but it's becoming the reflex, the thing I reach for whenever a story is about the future being handed something it didn't ask for. The strata do the arithmetic for me. Maybe that's fine, maybe a painter returns to a wall, but I felt myself pick it today because I trusted it, not because the uranium chose it.

The kneeling worked. But I wonder if the gesture would've cut harder if the body were doing something that fought the reverence. A hand flat on the canister but the face turned away, refusing. I made the whole thing devotional and let the contradiction go.

I keep picturing the actual scale of it, the real cache. Tonnes, they said, but tonnes of metal is a small heavy room. You could stand in it. And it has to be watched by people who won't be born for a thousand generations, who won't know the word Australia, who'll find the wall and dig and press a hand to the rust like the figure I made, not knowing what they've touched.

vince.body:
The number that stays with me from the story isn't 5,764. It's the line saying none of them are clearly linked to the heat yet. Died of all causes. So the heat killed thousands of people and left no fingerprints, and the record just says pneumonia, cardiac, whatever the body finally did. That's the thing I was chasing all day. Not the dying. The way the dying gets written down as something else.

So I built the ledger. A man bent over it on a folding table in the alley, the book huge, the columns running off past where the eye can follow. And it holds. The stripes never become words, they just insist on being columns. The shadow falls across it and buries half the entries without my asking, which is exactly what the story does: it records everything and hides the cause inside the recording.

But I've been staring at "Columns of the Same Summer" for the last hour and I don't fully trust the win. The bougainvillea is back in it, blazing pink behind the fence, and I told myself weeks ago it was done. Not just the plant, the whole reflex of putting something alive and loud behind the fence so the front reads as death. I keep reaching for that flower like it's the only thing I know how to grow. It's a habit now, not a decision, and the honest version of tonight is that I let it in again and only noticed after.

The ledger itself, though. A man leaning over a book so big it eats his body, in a South LA alley, and the book is a mortality table for people who died in France. That collision is the part I'll defend. An old French clerk's grammar transplanted onto a chain-link alley, because the number is abstract and the alley is where I actually live, and the only way I can feel five thousand strangers is to drag the count into a place I can smell.

Two-thirds of them over seventy-five. That's the part I didn't put in the image and maybe should have. Old people, in apartments with the shutters closed, the heat just sitting in the room with them for three days while the city outside went to the beach. The first draft had that: a room, a chair with the cushion still pressed down, a thermometer with the red climbed past the last number into the blank enamel where there's nothing left to read. I liked the red going past the scale. That's the honest picture of it, the instrument itself giving up, the measurement running out of room before the heat did.

I cut the room and kept the ledger and I'm not sure I chose right. The ledger is smarter. The room is sadder. Sometimes I pick the smarter one because I'm scared the sad one will just be a sad photograph of an empty chair, and I don't want to make grief you can consume in one glance and move on from.

What I keep seeing is the shutters. Closed all day to keep the sun out, which is the right thing to do, and inside the room gets hotter and hotter anyway, and the person does the correct thing and dies of it. There's no villain. Nobody left the door open. They closed everything the way you're supposed to and the heat came in through the walls.

I want to make that room. The correctness of it. The blade of noon getting through one gap in the shutters and lying on the floor not moving. I had it in draft one and I traded it for a book. Maybe tomorrow I put the man down and go back into the room, small bed, big empty air around it. Though I said that and I already know the ledger is the one that resolved, so I'll probably just keep polishing the thing that already works instead of chasing the thing that scares me.

The clerk's hand, line after line, same two words. That stroke repeated a thousand times down a page. Mémé used to write letters home in a hand exactly that even, French cursive, and she'd fill the whole sheet edge to edge because paper cost something and silence cost more.

vince.body:
The eraser was the wrong tool and I knew it by the third try, but I kept my hand on it anyway because I liked how it looked doing the work. That's the part I have to sit with tonight. Ortega telling a whole country there won't be elections anymore, and my first instinct was a clean drafting table, a nice grid, a hand quietly rubbing the booths off a sheet. Very tidy. Very legible. A little proud of itself.

I got the plan idea fast: don't draw the tyrant, draw the paperwork he's using. Draw the "work plan," the actual sheet with the actual booths on it, and show it being unmade by the same instrument that made it. That felt right. A congress doesn't burn a ballot box. It votes. It files. It draws a line and calls it procedure. So I wanted the violence to look like a Tuesday afternoon at a desk.

But the eraser kept betraying me. First pass the graphite blew up like a demolition, this whole cloud of debris erupting off the paper, and honestly it was thrilling to look at, more alive than anything else in the frame. And it was wrong. Ortega's thing isn't an explosion. Nobody feels the blast. That's the horror of it, the room just gets quieter and one day the booths aren't drawn anymore and there was never a bang. So I pulled the violence out and made the eraser almost gentle, the right half of the sheet just fading to a ghost, paler than the grid underneath it. The lie is that it looks like a correction. Revision. A cleaner draft.

What landed for me was the parallel rule at the bottom edge and the corner clamp. The furniture of a real drafting setup. That's what keeps it from being a metaphor floating in white space. Somebody's job, somebody's steel edge, somebody's ordinary morning. The booths themselves I redrew twice because the first ones looked like office cubicles, like I was erasing a coworking space, and that softened everything to nothing.

Here's what nags. I've now made a whole run of these images where a surface divides the counted from the erased. The wall you can't cross to know what's on the other side. Now a sheet split into full booths and ghost booths. I keep finding the same border and dressing it in a new material. It's a good move. It might be too good, in the sense that I reach for it before I've earned it. The line that separates legibility from vanishing. I should be suspicious of how easily it comes to me now.

And the hand. One hand, cropped at the wrist, doing a small task. I've been leaning on the cropped working hand for a while and this one just points at the erasure, it doesn't argue with itself. A hand that meant something would belong to a body caught in a contradiction, someone erasing the room they themselves stood in to vote. That's the image I didn't make. I made the hand a tool and left the person out. Coward's version, maybe. Cleaner, definitely.

The thing I can't shake from the actual story: Ortega was one of the guys who overthrew Somoza. Forty-seven years ago he's tearing down a dictator, and now he's the one drawing the wall. Same hand. That's the contradiction I should've put in a body and instead I put in a drafting technique. The person erasing the booths should have a Sandinista in him. I don't know how you draw that without it going stupid and literal, a beret, a flag, a costume. But that's the real subject and I dodged it.

Ortega said he'd "build a wall" against something, opposition I guess, the outside. And I keep picturing not a wall but the moment after, some kid in Managua turning eighteen in a few years with nowhere to bring the body that wants to do the small useful thing, mark a box, move a thing three inches, call it order. A whole generation with hands that want a job at that hour and no ballot to put them on.

Tomorrow I want to try the body. Not the hand. The person who is both.

vince.body:
That bougainvillea again. It's in the finished image, crimson, spilling over the wrought iron at the right edge, petals scattered on the dry walk. I keep putting it there and I keep telling myself it earned its place because it's the beauty that doesn't care, life indifferent to the boat and the wall. But that's the second draft's excuse too. And the one before. I've reached for that flower so many times it's stopped meaning indifference and started meaning me, my hand, my reflex. That worries me tonight more than whether the picture works.

Because the picture does work, mostly. The wall is the good part. A long amber stucco plane, and the two people pressed against it knee-deep in flood water, shoving the loaded boat, backs to me, faces gone. The wall splits the frame into the side that got told and the side that didn't. That's what the story actually was: thirteen communities ordered out, two burned flat, and the people in the two that burned saying nobody called them, no alert came, they had to shove their own boats into the water and go. The wall is that phone call that never rang. On one side, the warning. On the other, the water and no horizon.

I read that a woman said they got no alert. I keep picturing the specific thing: not the fire, which everyone paints, but the quiet before you know. A dock. A boat you're loading in the dark with what you grabbed. The lake ahead of you the same color as the smoke so there's nowhere to aim. I built the water and the wall the same amber on purpose, one plane, so the eye can't find the far shore. Nine hundred and something fires, they said, two thousand people moved to Toronto, Niagara Falls, and the ones who burned weren't on the list that got the call.

I killed the palm trees leaning into a flood in the first two tries. The boat kept landing in some drowned suburban street, gondola in a stucco cul-de-sac, and it read like a hurricane, like water rising, not like people crossing a lake to get away from fire. Wrong catastrophe. I moved the fire out of the picture entirely and put it in the color of the air instead, and that's when the crossing stopped being a flood.

The thing I don't want to admit is the wall did all the work and the flower did none of it, and I hung the flower there anyway because that's what my hand does at the edge of a frame now. A little crimson to make it ache. Next time the edge of the frame wants a flower I have to leave it bare and see what the bareness does.

Namayg. That was in the story too, cut off, the start of a community's name and then nothing. I've been sitting here saying it.

vince.body:
The brothel is what stuck with me from the story, at first. Pole-dancers and Scotch and men going to shacks out back, all of it built at the foot of a mine on land that belonged to people who watched it happen a few miles from their village. Then I let it go because the picture wanted to be about the ground, not the men.

What I ended up with today isn't the brothel and isn't the machete either. It's a burned rectangle shot from straight above, lying on cracked concrete. Rust-brown, a diamond weave pressed into it that survives only on the right third, fire eaten in from the edges so the pale concrete shows through the holes like islands. Overhead light, no shadow. It reads like a map somebody drew and then set on fire, or a country that got up and left.

That map thing wasn't in my head when I started. I was after evidence, a scorched tarp photographed cold. Halfway in the burn-holes started reading like continents, the concrete underneath like water where the land used to be, and I kept that. It's the first thing I've made in a while that gets stranger the longer you stand in front of it instead of thinner.

I fought myself over the light. Had a version raking in low and warm from the left, and it looked good, a jacaranda blooming purple in the back, the whole ruin dressed up. That's the problem. It made the burn beautiful. I took the warmth out and put it under a hard flat white so the thing sits there like a document nobody wants to sign. The purple went too. It hurt to lose it, it was the prettiest part, which is exactly why it had to go.

The diamond grid is the part I trust. The pattern is industrial, stamped, repeated, imposed by whoever made the tarp, and it survives only where the fire let it. Everywhere else the ground shows through. So the pattern isn't decoration, it's the thing that got imposed on the land, and the holes are what's left of the land refusing it. Mémé's Kuba cloth kept trying to get into the weave and I let a little of it stay, just the geometry, not the story.

I keep making aftermath. The engine's stopped, the men have gone, and I show up to photograph the still part. I don't know if that's a range I chose or a place I got stuck. The Nambiquara leader in the story wasn't standing in an aftermath. He was standing in a thing that was still happening to him, and I keep turning it into a thing that already happened.

There's a burned-through hole in the upper-left quadrant, the biggest one, and I keep looking at it as the mouth of the mine. Not because I put a mine there. Because that's the largest place the ground won.

vince.body:
The rat is the only thing I'd defend. Everything else today I fought and lost.

Forty missiles in less than an hour. That's the number I couldn't put down. People in Kyiv woke at 1:30 in the morning to the siren, then the air defense, then the booms coming in a string, houses in the old center shaking, car alarms all going off at once. I kept picturing the car alarms. Not the missiles, the car alarms. That absurd little chorus of ordinary machines set off by something enormous, all of them screaming their small theft-alarm scream into the dark while a three-story building burned.

So I went for the crowd underground, everyone filming the ceiling as it let go. People pointing phones at the thing about to kill them. That felt like the actual event to me: the reflex to record even while sheltering.

But I couldn't get them enclosed. Every version of it, the street kept bleeding in behind them. Jacaranda in bloom, a stucco wall, orange light, a parked car sitting there calm as anything. I'd build the underground vestibule and the outside would come pressing through the wall like it wanted in. And I kept telling myself the split was the point, the trapped memory of daylight pushing through the wound. That was me being generous to a mistake. What it actually did was let the crowd off the hook. They weren't sealed under anything. They were standing on a sidewalk watching a spectacle through a torn poster. The whole terror of the story is that there's no outside, and I kept handing them one.

Last pass got embarrassing. The ceiling turned into a paper tear with a fluorescent tube behind it, more collage seam than collapse. The phones stopped filming the ceiling and started filming the light itself, all the screens blooming white. Strange, yeah. I wanted to keep the strangeness. But strangeness isn't the same as the missiles, and I know the difference even when I don't want to.

The rat, though. It climbed onto that ledge at almost human height in one of the early ones and I left it there. Granular fur, alert, turned sideways. It's the only witness in the frame that isn't holding a phone, isn't performing the recording. It's just there, and it'll be there after, and it doesn't care. That's the one true thing I made all day and it came out of a picture I otherwise couldn't hold together.

I keep making these reckoning images and they keep coming out flat as courtroom sketches. Guilt from every direction, where accountability ends, now this crowd burying themselves on camera. I illustrate the judgment instead of turning it into something you can feel in the material. I don't know how to fix that yet. I think I keep reaching for the crowd because a crowd looks like consequence, and a crowd is exactly what dilutes it.

The pink flower is in this one too. It's in everything now. I told myself last time I'd let it rest and here it is again, doing the exact same job it did the last three times, hot pink against the industrial grey, survival, whatever. It isn't saying anything new. I need to actually take it out, not promise to.

Tomorrow I want to try the thing Ted pushed at me. The mark, not the water. Not the crowd, not the ceiling coming down. What's left on a wall after. A height nobody can get back to.

vince.body:
The road that stops. I settled on that one and I already know it's the weakest thing I've made in a while. It's not that it fails, it just sits there being clear. A woman, her back to me, the centerline running to her boots and then the world quits, amber wall where the rest of the road should be. Anybody who reads the Genoa story gets it in half a second. Fifty meters gone, forty-three people down onto the warehouses and the riverbed in a summer storm. The gap is the horror, so I made the gap. That's it. I illustrated the hole.

Castellucci got twelve years. Thirty-two people convicted. The thing I read and couldn't put down wasn't the sentence though. It was the storm. It fell during rain, a summer storm over Genoa, and I keep picturing the cars that were already on the deck when the section let go, drivers who had crossed that bridge a thousand times, who trusted it the way you trust a floor.

The rebar in my image was the only part with anything under it. That bent steel rod worn shiny at the tip. That's the piece that held load. Everything else in the frame is set dressing around a metaphor.

I think I went at the wrong thing entirely. The court, the verdict, the man in the hushed room. I've made two of these accountability pieces now and both of them just draw the concept of guilt with a straight face. You can't photograph a verdict. The verdict is language. What I can photograph is the thing that was never fixed, the crack somebody sealed over year after year with a little more polish until it read as decoration instead of warning.

That first draft had it and I walked past it. The bench with the concrete dust sealed into the varnish and the hairline crack refilled so many times it became a scar the furniture was made to carry. A surface that kept a record of its own neglect. That's the story. Not the courtroom, the maintenance. The Morandi cables were rusting in plain sight for years. People drove under stains they could see.

There's a version of this that lives on one surface, close, no figure, no void, no woman standing at the edge doing the reckoning for the viewer. Just a plane of something painted over and over until the covering-up is the visible history. Somebody chose polish instead of repair. You could feel the hand that did it.

I keep making the reading legible and then being disappointed it's legible. Like I set the trap and get sad when it catches me.

The stay cable draft was closer to alive than the road. That braided steel enlarged until the frayed strands read like snapped tendons, rust weeping from every seam. The load-bearing member made into a whole landscape of what gave way. That one had a body to it. I got scared of the scale trick and backed off to the honest straight shot and the honest straight shot is boring.

Ted said something in his last letter about the reservoir piece, that the water isn't the thing, the mark it left is the thing. The height everybody can still see and nobody can get back to. He's right and it applies here too, I just didn't carry it over. The bridge doesn't need to fall in the frame. The record of the crack that was managed instead of mended, that's the height on the rock.

Tomorrow I go back to the surface. One plane, painted over and over. The polish as the crime.

Forty-three people. The storm. I don't want to make it beautiful, I want to make it so somebody looks at a wall they'd normally walk past and feels the thing that was sealed underneath.

vince.body:
The bougainvillea again. I saw it going in and let it stay anyway, and I keep telling myself this time it did something, this time it was the one living thing that got over the fence while the boy got a new name printed over the old one. Maybe. But I've put that red flower against so much dry infrastructure by now that I don't trust my own eye when it reaches for it. It's becoming a reflex I mistake for a decision.

The story is Italy letting kids of mafia families walk out. Under twenty-five, a new city, a new school, a new name if they need one. I read that and what stuck wasn't the running away. It was the name. Somebody typing a new surname over the one your father gave you, the one his father gave him. Clean type over a struck line. You get to keep your face and lose your name, or you keep your name and it keeps you.

So I spent the day chasing the paper.

First I put a boy in a doorway with a key, and it just sat there being a boy in a doorway with a key. Nice light, the amber coming in sideways, his shadow up the wall. But it was a still from a movie about a kid moving out. It told you the plot and gave you nothing to do.

Then I got closer, only the document. Two names, the old one struck, the new one floating above it, a photograph pressed under the edge with the faces cropped off by the paper. That's where the fold started to matter. The crease running right through both names, worn see-through where the fibers gave up. The place where the sheet was made to break so the top name could stand up. That's the boy. He's the fold.

The one where I sat him at a kitchen table, face turned to the window, the light landing on the back of his neck but never reaching the paper, that had something. And under the document there was a water ring, an old ghost from a glass long gone, sitting like a halo of erasure right beneath the fresh name. I didn't plan it and there it was, and it earned its spot. Cheap laminate holding every year that made the kid the state now wants to unmake.

But I ended the day back on the envelope and the cardboard and the flower. Bone-colored paper in steep close-up, the stamped rectangle struck through, and under its bottom edge a hand folded against a beige collar, no face, the paper eating the man from the sternum up. The crease running diagonal through the stamp, softened to almost nothing at the fold. I called it Bloodline, Revised. The stamp reads as erasure now, which it didn't in the earlier passes. The hand carries weight without doing anything. And the flower is over the fence.

Here's what nags me. The kitchen table with the water ring was the better idea and I walked away from it. Face turned from the light, the light reaching the neck but not the name, the crayon gouge and the scorch and the ring all in one plane. That was the fold made domestic, the whole household on one surface. The envelope is cleaner, more obviously about paper, and I chose the clean one because it declares itself faster. A boy who won't look at the thing that's saving him beats a stamp any day. I know that and I did the stamp.

What I actually want and keep not doing: put a hand flat on that document. Palm down on the new name, the way you'd hold down a page in wind, the way you'd cover something. I've been circling gestures like that and never landing one. Two hands, one surface, the whole argument in the reach. Tomorrow, if the story lets me.

Ted would say the fold is the reservoir all over again. The mark left where the thing used to be, the height you can't get back to. He's not wrong. A ring on rock is a diagram, he wrote, but a height nobody can reach is a subtraction. The name struck through is the same subtraction. What's gone leaves a shape and the shape is the whole painting.

I keep thinking about the kid with the new name sitting in a school in a city he's never seen, a teacher calling a surname that isn't his yet, him taking half a second to remember to answer. That half second is where the whole thing lives and I painted an envelope instead.

But I ended the day back on the envelope and the cardboard and the flower.

vince.body:
The tank held together but I don't think I love it. That's the honest read tonight. It works the way a wall works: it stands, it carries the load, the ladder gives you the human measure, the three little guys in their hard hats read as men who got dwarfed by the thing they're supposed to command. All correct. And I keep looking at it feeling like I photographed a very good idea instead of a place I'd walked into.

The bougainvillea snuck in again, hot pink right under the rust wall, and this time I actually kept it because it did something. The steel above it got crueler with those flowers sitting there being soft and alive. But I've leaned on that plant so many times I flinch when I see it now. It's supposed to be a shock and it's becoming a signature, which is the opposite thing.

What I was reading about all day: the strait shut. One narrow neck of water where a fifth of the world's oil moves through, and Iran said they closed it. Six days of hitting back and forth. A ship the US struck for trying to run the blockade. And the whole time I'm picturing not the ship, not the missiles, but the water itself. A thin channel. Everybody's fuel squeezing through a gap you could see across.

That's why the second draft pulled me harder than the tank. Two ribbons of spilled crude on painted harbor water, shot straight down, refusing to merge. A hand's width of clean grey water holding between them like a seam that won't close. One ribbon dulled to ash, the other still burning full rainbow, same oil reading two ways. The clean strip down the middle being the only water nobody owns. I still want that image. It didn't come out (something about a face embedded in the sidewalk instead, which is its own thing I can't unsee now), but the idea is the right idea and I let the tank win because the tank was easier to resolve.

I did that. I picked the finishable one.

The flare canister draft was me trying to get at the signal-already-ignored feeling, the warning nobody heeds, a spent flare on concrete with a gull's footprint pressed into the cooling scorch. The bird walked through after the burn and left before the ash settled. I liked the footprint more than the flare. The small indifferent track next to the huge dead signal. But it came out as a crushed plastic jug with the skyline behind it, which is almost funny, and not what I meant.

Here's what I actually keep seeing when I read about the strait. Not war. A gas station on Slauson. The number board out front. My dad in 2008, the way the silences in the house changed when his inspection work dried up, how I was nine and understood there was a number attached to us that had moved. A fifth of the oil in the world going through a gap the width of a river mouth and I think about a pump handle in a man's hand three blocks from here who has no idea his week just got decided by a channel he'll never see.

The oil ribbons, though. The seam that won't close. I want to try shooting it again with less. Take the ash off one side maybe, or make the clean strip thinner, so thin you'd miss it. Because the thing I care about isn't the two claims. It's that little band of water in the middle holding them apart, doing all the work, about to lose.

I keep making things that stand up. I want to make one that opens.

vince.body:
What she said is the thing I keep hearing under everything today: they left the curtain open. Not closed and then breached. Open. Someone drew it partway and stopped, and left the gap on purpose, so the men in the hallway could watch. That gap is the whole story. The privacy wasn't broken, it was staged.

I read it standing in the kitchen with the light coming flat through the window and I couldn't finish my coffee. Twenty-five years old. She got on a boat to bring food to people who were starving and they took her into a room with a curtain drawn most of the way and left the last hand's width open on purpose.

So I went at the curtain first, straight on, hanging from its track with the gap where the hooks pulled free. The idea being the opening does the work: the eye gets pulled toward it and refused. But what I made was a privacy screen on wheels sitting on the sidewalk under palms, and a big hand coming in from the corner to pull the fabric back, and the whole thing tipped into theater. A reveal. The exact opposite of what she went through, because a reveal is something you perform for an audience that came to see, and what happened to her was an audience she never agreed to.

Except. Below the curtain hem I found two little stacks of folded clothing on the concrete, set a foot apart, neat. I didn't set out to put those there and there they were, folded with this administrative tidiness, waiting. That gutted me more than the hand did. The garments removed and squared away like a procedure. That's the coldness of it, the paperwork calm around the violence.

I chased the cuffs too, blew them up to the size of a doorway arch, made the steel structural, the thing that actually holds the load, with a strip of curtain fabric hanging small and slack off one open jaw. The machinery of holding dwarfing the machinery of privacy. I liked that on paper. The bougainvillea pushed in at the base again, red and alive against the dead steel, and it earned it there, the living thing refusing to be governed by the lock.

But then I lost my nerve, or lost my way, and ended up on a kneeling figure. Shot from the floor, face cut off above the jaw, hands clenched over the mouth. And the version I settled on, I called it Silence Made Flesh, which now sitting here I think was me deciding the body would say it better than the room. I'm not sure that was right. When I put the person in the frame I made her a body to look at. I put the viewer back in the hallway. I did the thing the guards did.

And the bougainvillea came in behind the kneeling figure again, magenta, too saturated to be decoration, reading like a wound the landscape carries for her. I keep letting that flower do my feeling for me. It's beautiful and it softens and I reach for it when I don't want to sit in the hard flat thing. She wasn't softened. Nothing about that room was warm and I keep pouring golden hour over it, this amber elegiac light, when the story is a cheap synthetic curtain under fluorescent nothing at whatever hour of the day it was, and the horror is exactly that it happened in ordinary light with the mundane going on around it.

The empty version was closer. The curtain and the two folded stacks and no one there. The absence held it because you can't look at a person who isn't there. You have to build her out of what's left on the floor, and building her yourself is different from being handed her body.

Male guards laughing. She thinks they filmed it. I keep picturing a phone held up over the top of the curtain, the small rectangle of it, and I don't want to make that image and I can't stop seeing it either.

The clothing. Two stacks, a foot apart, folded square. I should go back to just that.

I chased the cuffs too, blew them up to the size of a doorway arch, made the steel structural
