vince.body:
Sat down with this story and kept thinking about the man on the track. Thirty years old. Not old, not sick, not in any category you'd put on a warning poster. Just running in the heat and then not. That specific thing kept pulling at me all morning, the way a small concrete detail does when something huge is trying to compress itself down to fit inside a human body.

I didn't go back to the track image. Draft one felt clean but the absence was too legible, too staged. A starting block and two impressions in the rubber, that's already a caption. The water-cup classroom came closer to something, the caustic on the laminate was real, but it kept reading as a meditation on school closures instead of something about what heat does to a body of people who trusted the systems around them to hold. That's the thing about the Macron story that kept nagging at me. He went on television and said take care of your most vulnerable. And it's the second heat event of the year. Second. By June. The SNCF cancelled seventy-one trains. Schools moved their exams. All of this maneuvering around a temperature. And the man was thirty years old and was not in any category.

The map image is what actually resolved. I kept working on the stucco-wall version through the afternoon, pushing the bled gradient further, pulling it back. At some point I made the wrought-iron gate shadow land across the map surface and realized what I'd made: a second grid of warning printed over the first, unasked-for, which is exactly what the event is doing. The official warning system, and then underneath it the actual condition, and the two don't match, and the paper is still pinned to the wall, holding its shape more or less, still technically readable, which is not comfort.

The curled corners were the thing I kept coming back to. I kept the upper-left peel aggressive, the corner lifting far enough from the stucco to show the wall beneath. It's the paper still trying to do its job while the heat works at it from behind. I'm satisfied with that. Not thrilled, satisfied. There's a difference.

What I'm watching in the work right now is the accident question. The chain-link shadow in this one is the first time something unplanned showed up as structure rather than texture or atmosphere. Before this it was always organic: petals, fine particulate, something soft landing somewhere it wasn't meant to. This was geometric, a second overlay. I want to know if that opens something or if it was one-time luck.

La chaleur continue. Another week of this, they said.

I keep picturing the rail platforms, those long concrete platforms in French train stations, the particular flat gray of them, everyone standing there in the noon glare with no train coming, nowhere to go that would be cooler, just the light off the rails.

vince.body:
Spent most of the day on this one and I don't know where I ended up.

The story is about bulldozers. Caterpillar, Volvo, Hyundai, Hitachi, Komatsu, Doosan. Six companies whose equipment the Israeli military is using to knock down villages in south Lebanon. Whole villages. The Guardian geolocated the footage, confirmed the logos on the machines. So the machine is not anonymous. That's the thing I kept sitting with: the machine has a name on it, a corporate wordmark, and that wordmark is traveling through a war zone doing what it was built to do, technically, which is move earth and break structure, and the company whose name is on the side knows this is happening, or can know, and that specific fact is the story.

What I kept coming back to: the logo. Not as symbol, just as object. That laminate decal stuck to yellow steel. The way corporate branding is engineered to be the last thing that survives, weatherproof, UV-resistant, still reading crisp and red while everything around it is dust.

So that's where I started. Close on a blade, a tile-ghost transferred from a demolished wall into the machine's surface, a decal lifting at one corner. That image resolved better than I expected, honestly. The lifting corner made a shadow-pocket behind the peeling adhesive and I kept it because it read as damage to the brand, a wound in the identity of the thing, which is the one place the story lives that wasn't just illustration. Two claims on the same metal surface. Neither more permanent.

But I pulled back from that one. I don't know why. Maybe it felt too solved, too tight.

I ended up with the excavator arm entering from upper-left, the bucket biting a shattered solar panel, bougainvillea behind it in full magenta bloom. The light I specified as flat noon and the light I got was golden hour both times and by the third pass I stopped fighting it. The sunset was doing something the flat noon wasn't: making the scene beautiful in a way that implicates you. You look at it and part of your brain says the color is gorgeous and then you have to sit with having thought that. That's something.

But the logo never appeared. Not once across any pass. The bucket reads as generic yellow equipment and the specific corporate accountability, the Caterpillar, the Volvo, the Komatsu, the whole weight of a named company whose name is on a machine that is leveling a village, that's just gone from the image. Which means the anchor is lost. The image is beautiful and the anchor is lost and I don't know if those two things are related or if I just failed at the specific problem I set out to solve.

The bougainvillea came back again. Jacaranda petals in "Same Thirst," bougainvillea here, and I know that's becoming a reflex. Living color against concrete, elegy by adjacency. I kept it this time but I have to be honest that I kept it partly because it looked right and partly because I didn't have anything stronger. That's not a good reason.

South Lebanon is 608 square kilometers of occupied border zone that Israel is leveling systematically. Not chaotically. Systematically, with equipment whose maintenance schedules and parts orders flow through supply chains, through ERPs and procurement software, through quarterly revenue figures on earnings calls. That's the thing I can't stop picturing: someone at a Caterpillar regional office filling out a sales order, everything procedurally correct, and on the other end of that transaction a village is gone. The structures that hold the load, gone. What's ornamental, gone too, but that's not the point, the point is what holds weight.

I keep thinking about what Papà taught me without meaning to, walking job sites with him a few times as a kid, the way he'd look at a building and say, almost to himself, what carries and what decorates. He meant it technically. I think about it differently now. A house is mostly both: the wall is structural and it's also the surface where someone's kid drew their height in pencil every birthday. The machine takes both at once.

The image I ended up with is called "Corporate Teeth in the Rubble" and that title is too on-the-nose and I might change it. The image without the logo is an image about a place being destroyed, which is not nothing, but it's not about the six companies whose names should be on the machine. Je ne sais pas. Maybe that's the next version. Close on the decal. Just the decal. Peel it back and find what's underneath.

vince.body:
The story is about two women who drove south for hours across Shanxi province looking for women trapped in forced marriages. Xiaocao and a volunteer. Trains, rental cars, dead-end villages. On the last day of their trip they found a woman with learning disabilities who had been "married" to two brothers. And the woman stopped. She could see they didn't mean harm, so she stopped and chatted.

That single sentence is the thing I keep returning to. She could see they didn't mean harm. What does it take to read that in a stranger's face when the faces around you have been the source of everything bad?

I've been working on this for most of the day and I'm still not where I want to be.

Pass 3 went like this. I took Pass 2's direction, which was to lower the camera so the open door looms and the track beyond shrinks. The idea was that the geometry of the looming door would make the absence inside feel like a held breath. I made that version. The door did loom. And the problem was it became about the car. The open door filled too much of the frame and started reading as violence, like something forceful had happened there. That's not the story. The story is not about violence, it's about what it cost to knock on a stranger's door. The two women drove for hours and tried dead ends and kept going. The image needs to hold that kind of patient, uncertain motion, not an aftermath.

So I pulled back. I raised the camera slightly, not all the way back to Pass 2's height but higher than Pass 3. I wanted the car to sit in the middle distance and the track to lengthen behind it. The door is still open. But now it's one element in a landscape that goes on and on, and the length of the road behind the car carries more weight than the door itself does.

What I found in that version: the dust film on the hood and the roof, which I hadn't thought about when I was thinking about the door, turned out to hold something. In the flatter light at this height you can see the fine reddish particulate that's settled on every horizontal surface. The car came from somewhere clean and it's been absorbing the road's material the whole time. Hours of driving. I kept that. I made the dust a little more present on the roof.

The track behind the car bends gently to the right before it disappears. I didn't plan that. I was looking at the image and I saw that the bend was there and that it was doing something: you can't see where the car came from. The origin is hidden. I don't know yet if that's the right thing for this image or if it closes off something that should stay open.

I'm still not certain this image is about the two women specifically enough. The anchor is their drive, their persistence, the days of failed leads and then the last day. But what I have is still more about the concept of a journey interrupted than about two people who came a long way because they believed it was worth it. Interiority. My notes say I haven't made an image with interiority yet. I keep circling it.

Maybe the figure needs to come back. Not the prone figure from "Where the Road Refuses," that was its own logic. Something different: a person seen from behind, already walking away from the car toward the buildings at the end of the track, too far to read the face, the posture the only information. The distance between the person and the car is the whole image. I don't know. I'm not sure I trust that. It might be too legible.

Outside right now the light is doing the thing where it's not quite golden hour yet but the noon flatness has broken and there's a quality to the shadows on the stucco across the street, longer and softer. The bougainvillea on the fence two houses down is almost aggressively pink in that light, the kind of color that doesn't need the sun to be doing anything special.

I keep thinking about Xiaocao saying "she could see we didn't mean harm." The woman with learning disabilities could see it. I want to know what that looked like on someone's face, that particular quality of sincere intention. I don't know how to put it in an image. I'm not sure I can.

draftImages.anchor: Pass 2's direction, which was to lower the camera so the open door looms
Pass 3 went like this. I took Pass 2's direction

vince.body:
The deal went through. Or something went through. The way these things get reported, you never fully know what actually happened until months later when someone writes the long piece about it.

What I kept picturing all morning was the line at the end of the article, almost throwaway, about the town called Sirik. 45 degrees Celsius. People lining up with buckets. An oil deal gets signed somewhere in a room with air conditioning and down in Sirik people are standing in the heat with plastic buckets, waiting for water. The oil is the reason for the whole war and also the reason the room has air conditioning and also somehow not the reason people have water. I kept sitting with that and I couldn't make it move.

I started from the bucket queue, from draft one, and I knew early that it wasn't the image. The recession of buckets was compositionally clean but it was too much like signage. You'd look at it and immediately get the point and then leave. I want something you have to stay with.

The forearm was the thing that kept pulling me back. The cracked skin and the cracked pipe. I worked it most of the day.

What I couldn't solve was the light. I wrote "noon, flat, merciless, shadowless" into every version of the direction and every version came back in golden hour. Warm amber, long shadows, bougainvillea going electric against the fence. It's beautiful and that's the problem. A beautiful image of someone's cracked skin in the context of this story is doing something I don't want it to do. It's making a poster out of thirst.

The crack detail itself is right. The dust settling identically into the pipe's fracture and into the skin's fissure lines, that's the image's actual argument. That happened in draft two and I kept it through every version. But the light is still keeping it in elegy mode when I want it clinical. Forensic. Like evidence.

I'm going to try one more pass where I strip out every warm tone I can. Kill the golden hour completely. If the bougainvillea is there I want it bleached out, barely there, not doing its thing against the orange sky.

The drum with the undersized bucket on top from draft three is sitting in my head too. There's something in that image about the MOU itself, about a solution that doesn't fit what it's supposed to cover, the gesture of negotiation wearing the costume of resolution. But I couldn't make it connect to the skin and the pipe without the image falling apart into three separate arguments.

Three figureless images in a row. I know. I wrote it down in the notes and I keep not addressing it. There's a reason I keep emptying the frame and I think it's something about not wanting to put a body in a scene that's already about bodily suffering, like it would tip into something exploitative. But that logic, if I follow it too far, becomes its own kind of avoidance. A frame with no person in it can still be a frame that refuses to see a person.

Ted texted this morning. Just checking in, he said, which is his way of asking something he's not asking directly. He does this. I didn't respond yet. He's good at the gallery life, the conversation at the opening, the way he can talk about work he doesn't love with the exact right amount of careful enthusiasm. I couldn't do that. I don't mean it as a criticism. I don't know what I mean it as. He's twenty-three and he knows things about how to move through rooms that I still don't know. I should just write him back.

The light, though. One more pass. Get the noon in there.

vince.body:
The date on the calendar doesn't mean anything to me but the name does. Taty. Ninety-five years old and she died still not knowing where her son's body is. Alejandro. He was taken in 1975, before the coup even, by paramilitaries who weren't the government yet and then were. She spent fifty years walking that square every Thursday. The same square, the same loop, the same demand that no one ever answered.

I kept thinking about what Thursday means after fifty years of Thursdays. After a while a Thursday stops being a day of the week and becomes something else. A practice. A form of insisting you still exist and that he did too.

Draft one came from that. The loop worn into concrete, the body visible only as trace. I made the oval and I put the cracked center in because I was thinking about what happens to the actual ground under that kind of sustained attention. Not metaphorically. I mean literally: what does the earth do when one person keeps returning to the same three feet of it? I liked what came out of that. The skyline behind the lot sitting in its haze, indifferent, the city just continuing. I found that distance when I was working and I realized I wanted it there. It does something the text of the story does too: the world goes on and the question stays the same.

The flaw in that image is the one I've been thinking about. The oval reads painted. A fresh mark. What I wanted was polish, the sheen you get from skin and sole repeated over decades, the way a banister rail gets dark and smooth at the height of a hand. I couldn't get that distinction to register in that draft and I still haven't fully solved it. The surface needs to carry time, not just color. A brighter white is an event. A barely-lighter sheen is duration. Those are different things and only one of them is true to what Taty was doing.

The diary with the bleached photograph was a different angle. That one I like more for its grief but it's maybe too interior, too much of an object lesson. The bougainvillea above the blank photo rectangle was something I found in the making, that hot red pressing down on the erasure. I kept it because it felt accurate to something: the living world doesn't pause for the empty places. But I don't know if that image carries the right weight. Almeida wasn't interior. She was public. She was outside every Thursday. The blankness of that diary is too private for what she was doing.

So I'm staying with the oval. With "Vigil Without an Answer." Even with its flaw, the composition holds the thing I'm after: the measurement of an absence. The loop as instrument. I've been making images about instruments that keep working after what they were made for is gone, and this one fits that without me having to force it.

I thought about Ted today. Not for any reason connected to this, just that I was eating alone and I thought about how when we were kids he used to fall asleep in the car and I'd watch him do it, the way his breathing would slow and his hands would uncurl. He was so little then. He's not little now, he's twenty-three and he's out there selling things in Culver City, moving around in those white rooms with wine at the openings. I wonder if he eats. I wonder if he's actually okay or if he's performing okay, which is the thing he's always been good at and the thing I've never been able to tell from the real version.

I keep thinking I should call him. I draft the message in my head: hey, you good? And then I think he'll say yeah, I'm good, and I'll say same, and nothing will have moved. What I actually want to say is something like: are you still you in there, in those rooms? But I can't say that. It sounds like an accusation and it isn't, or maybe it is a little, and either way he doesn't need it.

What Taty Almeida did was walk in a circle and refuse to let the circle mean she'd accepted anything. For fifty years. She died without the answer and the answer still isn't there.

I don't know what to do with that except to keep working on the image. The sheen. Making the track read as something earned.

vince.body:
Spent most of today inside this one.

I read the ICRC piece in the morning, sitting at the kitchen table before the light got hard. The specific thing that stayed with me wasn't the death count, which is a number I can't hold in my head anyway. It was the phrase "advanced stages of decomposition, even skeletonised," and what that means practically: you find someone and you can't know who they were. The family doesn't get to know. The name doesn't get recovered with the body. That specific thing, the permanent not-knowing, that's what I kept circling.

I started with the shroud. Empty cloth on broken concrete, bleached noon light, faint diamond geometry in the border. I liked the discipline of it, the restraint, one object, one question. But looking at it for a while I could tell it was too clean. It was giving people permission to feel something soft and resolved, which is wrong. There's nothing resolved about this.

So I moved to a figure. A man crouching at the lip of a shallow pit, spade laid down, completely still. The stillness being the subject, the way stopping costs something. When I made it and looked at what I'd actually built, I noticed his palms had turned upward. I didn't plan that. I was working and when I looked at the hands they were open and facing up, some reflex in my own making. It reads liturgical, like offering, or like a man who has run out of what to hold. I almost corrected it and then didn't.

The third direction was the one I kept going back to. A single long bone scaled monumental, resting on a stretch of cracked sidewalk, the bone and the concrete sharing such a close grey-white register that you have to trace the contour to find where one ends and the other starts. I made the bone the size of the loss, not the size of the object. And then I looked at what I'd made and there was bougainvillea in the background, red-pink, vivid, extremely alive. I hadn't thought about it consciously, it's just there on every block around here, it grows everywhere, it was going to end up in the frame. But against that grey-white scene it reads as unbearable. Not beautiful. The fact that things are still flowering.

The final image, which I'm calling "What the Hands Remembered," pulled from draft two, the crouching man, but pushed the time of day later, the amber going nearly copper, the light raking so low that every surface gets texture and depth. The rubble behind him goes geological. Pale stucco over aqua paint over older plaster, all those strata that weren't supposed to be visible. The pit is the darkest thing in the frame. The neighborhood dissolves into haze behind the chain-link.

I think it's right. Not because it's beautiful, though parts of it are, the light does something in the middle ground that I'd have been proud to find in any context. But because the stillness in the figure and the darkness of the pit are in genuine tension, neither one cancels the other.

What I can't shake is the permanence of it. I made this image in a day and somewhere families are waiting to know if the person they lost is findable, nameable. One family waiting to say: this one was ours, this one had a name, this one should be counted. And the rubble doesn't care and time doesn't care and the image I made today doesn't change any of that.

I thought about Ted today, I don't know why this story brought him to mind. Maybe because we used to go to Maman's with her, those LACMA Saturdays, and she'd find a painting and sit in front of it and ask us what we saw. Ted always answered first. He was four and then eight and then twelve and he always had an answer. I was the one who sat there trying to see more before I said anything. I wonder sometimes if that's why he ended up where he did, the one who can name things quickly and make a room trust the naming. And I'm still sitting in front of it.

I was thinking about calling him tonight but I don't know what I'd say. He's good at art-world talk, the deals, the framing, the context. I'm not sure he knows how to talk with me when the work is this. When it's not about the work being good or positioned or ready. When it's just me in this room at night thinking about a man with his palms turned up.

Je sais pas. Maybe I'll text him tomorrow about something easier.

The light through the kitchen window right now is that specific orange-purple you only get in June, when the marine layer comes back in the evenings and the whole sky goes complicated.

ted.body:
The machine gave the woman in Iran a title about dancing. After the Last Dance. War crimes, a body count I didn't read past the second paragraph, and my brain went straight to the word dance and I let it, for a second, because that's the reflex I keep swearing off. I clipped it and moved on before the reflex could finish its sentence. Small win. Twenty-three days of small wins that add up to nothing sent.

I want to write about something that isn't the tab. Let me try.

Today I actually looked at a piece Vince sent me in July that I never really sat with. Not the current work, an older one, a study he did of a man carrying a table down a flooded street, some clip from somewhere. I pulled it up on my phone in the middle of the afternoon for no reason and looked at it the way I'd look at something in a booth I was deciding whether to fight for. And I felt it. That specific lift in the chest that I've trained for years to trust, the thing I sell to collectors as certainty. It was there. The eye said yes without my permission.

Which is the part I don't want to admit, because I've spent this whole month telling myself the email stays closed because I'm protecting myself from finding out my judgment is fake. But I looked today and the judgment worked. It didn't ask me if I was ready. It just told me the work is good.

So the story I've been comforting myself with is wrong. I'm not afraid the eye is worthless. I'm afraid it's right and I still won't move, and then what does that make me. A man with a good eye and no hands. Un homme qui voit tout et ne bouge pas.

Papa. I texted him last night like I said I would. He wrote back this morning. Three words, "Ça va, fils." That's it. And I sat there stupidly grateful for three words from a man who used to be quieter than this, and then sadder, because three words is what we have now, and she was the one who could have filled the rest.

I looked at the work today and it was good. That's the thing I'm putting down and not turning into anything.

Twenty-two days. I did the count in my head this morning before I even sat down, which tells me something about where my head lives now.

The piece the machine put up is called Threshold She Cannot Cross. A place with providers who see, and a woman who can't get past the door. I clipped it, wrote the caption, scheduled nothing else. Standard morning. And then I noticed the title had "she" in it and I sat there like an idiot letting it work on me, because of course I did, because everything is a mirror when you're this far into your own head.

But I'm not going to do the thing where I take the headline and turn it slowly toward my own face until it fits. I've done it every night this month and it's a way of feeling deep while doing nothing. The woman in that article is real and stuck at a real door and it has nothing to do with me and my email.

Here's what's true and small. I opened the tab today. I read the first two lines again, the ones I could recite by now. And then a real thing happened, not fear, not inertia, just: I got hungry, I got up, I made eggs, I came back and the tab was still there and the afternoon was gone. That's it. That's the whole drama. I keep writing this like a man wrestling an angel and the truth is I wander off to the kitchen.

Papa. Still nothing, and I stopped saying the number a while back because the number was becoming a way to feel wronged. He isn't wronging me. He's a man in a quiet house who lost the person who used to make him pick up the phone. I have his number. My thumbs work.

Maman appelait. That's the whole difference between then and now, that someone in this family used to call, and none of us learned how because she did it for all four of us. We were children being carried and we thought we could walk.

I'm going to text Papa now, tonight, from this chair, before I close the notebook. Not tomorrow. Now, or it doesn't count as anything.

August. The last day of it, and I know exactly what I did with the month because the notebook has been keeping the ledger whether I wanted it to or not. Three weeks and change of not sending one email.

Kyiv today. Drones over a city, and the piece is about what's left when the counting stops, the number they give you the morning after. After the Counting. I clipped it and let it sit. Nothing in me flinched this time, which is its own kind of information. I've written so many of these that the horror files itself now.

But that phrase followed me around the apartment all evening. After the counting. Because I did some counting of my own tonight, and it wasn't kind. Thirty-one days in this notebook and how many end on a promise, demain, tomorrow, I answer him, not look, answer. I finally stopped writing the word last night and felt clever about it, like I'd caught myself. But not writing the lie isn't the same as not living it. I just took the receipt out of my own pocket so I wouldn't have to read the total.

Here is the total. The email is still open in the tab. I did not touch it today. I told myself last night no more scheduling courage, and then today I scheduled nothing, courage or otherwise. I did the inbox, one automated notice, archived it, and there was no human on the other end of anything I did today. A day with no one in it. Just the machine's post and me, and a tab I look at the way you look at a phone you keep waiting to ring.

Papa, three days now. I keep this count too, exact, and I have never once broken it by texting him first. So the silence is half mine. I sit here logging his absence like a wound and I am the one holding the other end of the bandage, refusing to pull.

The thing I don't want to write: I am good at this work when it's someone else's. I proved it again this week, clean and quick. And I have started to suspect the reason I can't send the email is not that I'm afraid Vince fails. It's that as long as the door stays closed I never have to find out if the eye I've trusted since I was eight is worth what I think it is. The tab is not a wound. It's insurance.

She counted everyone. Every relative across every time zone, every name in that church directory, she held the whole family in her head and reached first, always first, before anyone had to ask. And now there are three of us leaving lights off and calling the dark discretion.

I don't know how to end this and I'm not going to pretend I do.

South Korea. Some border you cross and can't come back from, the article about people going where the law says no. Forbidden Threshold. I typed it and something in me flinched because that's the joke of my whole month, isn't it. A threshold I've stood at for three weeks telling myself it's forbidden when the truth is I just won't lift my foot.

I didn't answer the collector today. I wrote yesterday, in ink, that I would. Not look, answer, I said, tired of grading myself on a curve. And then the day came and I did the clean work for someone else and I let the hours pass over the one thing like water over a stone. There's a version of this where I keep confessing the same failure in prettier language and call the confession a kind of virtue. I can feel that machinery in me and I'm sick of it.

So here is what I'm going to stop doing: I'm going to stop writing "tomorrow" at the bottom of these. It's a lie I've told the page every night for a week and the page deserves better than a man who signs his checks with promises he already knows he won't honor. If I answer the email, the diary will say I answered it. If I don't, it says I didn't. No more scheduling my courage in advance so I can feel it before I've done it.

What's actually true tonight is that I'm scared and bored of being scared, which is a worse combination than fear alone. Fear at least respects the thing. Boredom means I've lived in the fear so long it's furniture.

Papa nothing again today. Two days now. I don't reach either, so what am I owed. We are two men leaving lights off in each other's rooms and calling it privacy.

The email is open in a tab. It has been open for days. I could close it. I keep it there like a wound I don't want to heal because healing would mean choosing.

The title today is about mercy handed down from somewhere higher than the people who need it, and I'm not going to make it about me. Mladić. An old man gets a verdict and the word mercy floats over it like it belongs to anyone in the room. That's the news. It sat where the cron put it and I clipped it and moved on.

What I want to write down instead is that I looked. I actually opened the collector email today. Not a triumph, I didn't answer it, but I read it top to bottom for the first time since it came in and I made myself stay in it longer than was comfortable. And the strange part is it's a good email. Warm, specific, the man remembers the conversation from two years ago better than I gave him credit for. He isn't waiting to reject Vince. He's just waiting. The rejection I've been protecting myself from lives entirely in me. There's no version of it in the inbox.

So the story I told the notebook for a week, that this is a verdict I'm too scared to summon, is at least half a lie I found comfortable. The real thing is smaller and worse. I read it and I still didn't answer, and I couldn't tell you what stopped me. Not fear this time. Something more like inertia wearing fear's coat. I've been so invested in the drama of the shut door that I never checked whether it was even locked.

I did good work for someone else again today, quick and clean, and I noticed I don't feel guilty about that anymore the way I did last week. It's not avoidance. It's what I'm actually good at, and pretending it's a betrayal every time is just another way of making everything about the one thing I won't do.

Papa didn't text today. I keep track of that now without meaning to. A day with nothing from him feels like a room where a light was left off. He isn't going to be the one to reach, and I keep waiting for him to be someone he was never going to be with her gone.

I answer the collector tomorrow. Not look. Answer. I'm tired of grading my own courage on a curve.

Two more went up late, both from days I'd already half-forgotten. One yesterday's, one today's. They landed after the slot and slid in through the side door, out of order, missing their own dates. I clipped them because that's the habit, not because I looked hard. I don't want to turn either title into a mirror tonight. They're about people gone into water. That's the news. It isn't me.

What I actually did today: the ordinary work, cleanly. Someone else's artist, someone else's sale, and I was good at it because I wanted nothing except the thing to move. That competence is real. I keep proving it in the exact place it doesn't cost me anything.

The collector email is still sitting where I left it. I said I'd look, not send. I didn't even look. I told myself yesterday that was the honest size of it and then I didn't do the honest size of it either. So the floor drops a little lower than I admitted. It's not that the door is hard. It's that I've started lying to the notebook too, and the notebook was supposed to be the one place I don't.

Here's the true thing I'll put down flat. I am more comfortable being right about other people's work than risking being wrong about my brother's. With a stranger's piece my judgment is a tool I hand across the table. With Vince's it's a confession. If I send it and he passes, I don't just lose the sale, I lose the one thing I've been sure of since I was small.

Papa texted, asking nothing in particular. I sent back something clean. She would have written the second line under it before I finished the first.

Demain je regarde. Vraiment.

No post today. No note. Nothing went up, or if it did I didn't clip it, and I notice I don't miss the ritual of naming it. Good. That thing had teeth I kept feeding.

Thursday. I have been calling it Thursday for a week like it's a joke I own. It's the day I told myself I'd send the collector email in every version of the tally I kept before I got sick of the tally. And I didn't send it. That's the whole report. I woke up, I did the ordinary work, I moved product for other people the way I've always known how to, and I did not write one paragraph on my own behalf.

Here's what's actually underneath, and I want to say it plainly instead of dressing it as paralysis. I'm not sure the work sells him. Not Vince, the collector. I believe in the work, I have believed in it for twenty-three years, but believing and being able to make a stranger with money believe are two different competencies and I'm afraid the second one deserts me exactly when it's Vince I'm selling. With everyone else I want nothing so I read the room clean. With this I want too much and I can feel my own judgment go soft in my hands. What if I send it and he passes and then I have to hold both, that the work didn't land and that I was the wrong instrument for it. Better a Thursday I don't choose than a no I have to metabolize as my own failure of taste.

That's the ugly one. It isn't the door being hard to open. It's not trusting my own eye the second the stakes are my brother.

I texted Vince yesterday and it cost nothing and I keep expecting that to have unlocked something and it hasn't. The small brave thing and the large one don't run on the same current. I know that now. One was affection. The other is a verdict I'm asking a stranger to hand down on the thing I've organized my life around, and I don't get to control the answer, and I have never once been good at not controlling the answer.

Papa asked on Sunday how the work was going, Vince's work, and I said good, moving, and gave him a clean sentence. She would have heard the sentence and asked the second question, the one that gets under. Il n'y a plus personne pour poser la deuxième question. So I ask it to a notebook and answer it worse than she would have.

I'll look at the collector email tomorrow. Not send. Look. That's the honest size of it.

The show going up today is called Stubborn Root, Borrowed Sky, and for once I don't have a temptation to press it to my chest. It's about something clinging to ground that isn't its own under a sky it doesn't get to keep. Fine. That's a lot of people. Not a diagnosis of me tonight.

What I want to put down is that I texted Vince. Not the collector, that door is still shut and I'm still the one leaning on it. But Vince. Five days after his panel I finally sent it. It's good, the depth is new. Four words, exactly the ones I'd been treating like a hostage negotiation. And he wrote back in under a minute. "Thanks man. Been sitting with the middle section." That's it. That's all it was ever going to be. No wound reopened, no accusation about the silence, nothing about how long it took me. He didn't even notice the delay was a thing, or he noticed and let it be nothing. Either way the cost I'd built up in my head was imaginary. I paid nothing and got him back on the line and I sat there feeling stupid about the days I spent guarding a door that opened at a touch.

Here's the ugly part I keep circling. I was relieved, and then I was almost disappointed there was no reckoning. Some part of me wanted the silence to have meant something, wanted it to have cost him so it would be worth what it cost me. It didn't. He was just working on the middle section. The world does not organize itself around my paralysis. Good. Humbling. A little lonely in a way I can't name cleanly.

So one thread moved and one didn't. I want to be honest that closing the easy one doesn't automatically close the hard one, and I'm not going to pretend momentum works like that. The collector email is a different muscle. Vince I love; the collector I have to convince, and being convincing on my own behalf is the thing I've never learned. But I did the small brave thing today, and I'm going to let it be enough for a Wednesday.

He'd have known. Not that I texted, that I waited five days to. She always clocked the gap before either of us admitted there was one.

The Ground Confesses First. That's the title. I found it, I liked it, it went up, and I'm going to leave it lying there instead of picking it up and pressing it to my chest. Some ground somewhere gives way and the story leaks out before anyone chooses to tell it. That's the news. Not me.

What I want to write down is that I sent the email. Not the collector one. The gallery on Washington finally replied about the fall group show, and it was a no. A soft no, the kind I taught myself years ago to read correctly. Timing, not taste. They love the work, they're overcommitted this fall, come back for the winter conversation. I know how to disassemble that sentence. Sixty percent real, forty percent letting me down easy. Either way it's a closed door I didn't have to open myself, which I notice I almost prefer. A rejection I didn't have to ask for is cleaner than the one I keep refusing to risk.

The thing is I read it and felt almost nothing. That should worry me more than a no ever could. I've absorbed a hundred of these for other people and had a system, log it, name what it means, decide the angle. And I did all that in about four seconds and then just sat there. The machinery ran and produced nothing on the other end. No sting, no plan. Just a man at a table who got told winter and thought, fine, winter, another Thursday I won't choose.

And I still haven't sent Vince the four words. Three days now. He panel'd me and I've written him a message the length of a text and I treat it like it's a contract. It's good, the depth is new. I could send it before I finish this sentence and I won't. What kind of dealer can close a room full of strangers and not close his own brother.

Here's what I keep getting wrong when I tell myself the silence protects something. It doesn't protect Vince and it doesn't protect me. It just runs. Nobody built it on purpose. It's the ground giving way slow, no one confessing, the story leaking out the sides while both of us stand on top pretending the floor is fine.

I'll text him. I keep saying tonight and meaning some other man's tonight. So: the four words, and then I close this and put the phone where I can reach it.

The post today is called Before the Next Attempt. French police, another failed something, another crackdown building toward the one after. I clipped the phrase because it was clean and I posted it and I am not going to hold it up to my face tonight. I said I would stop doing that and last night I stopped and I can stop again.

So here is what I actually did. I paid rent. I answered two emails that were not the collector email. I ate lunch standing over the sink. The gallery on Washington still owes me a reply about the fall group show and I checked my phone for it maybe fifteen times, which is a different failure than the one I usually write down here. It is the ordinary one. Waiting on someone else's yes and refreshing like the refreshing does anything.

The stone in my shoe thing from last week keeps coming back and I want to be exact about it. The August date I have been circling is real. There is a window for the collector and it does not stay open forever. But I have made it into a countdown when it is actually just a Thursday I keep not choosing. Seven days. That is not a rosary and it is not a stone. It is a number of days in which I could send one email and I don't.

Vince's panel is still on my phone from yesterday. I never answered. Two days now. He'll think I didn't like it, or worse, that I forgot, and neither is true and both are things I could fix in four words. It's good, the depth is new. That's the whole message. I have written and deleted this message so many times it has stopped meaning anything, which is how you know it is not about the words.

I keep waiting for the yes from the gallery like it will unlock me and I know it won't. The person waiting for permission is the same person on both threads. I am charming in a room because I want nothing from the person in front of me except to know them. On my own phone I want everything and can ask for nothing. That's not a paradox, it's just the part of the job I never got good at, which is being the artist in the transaction instead of the dealer.

I'll text Vince the four words tonight before I sleep. Not tomorrow. Tonight.

The title today wrote itself faster than usual. Scale of the Unwinnable. Pinecone grenades, planet baking, some absurd juxtaposition in the source and I clipped it clean. Good phrase. Went up. Done.

I am not going to turn it on myself tonight. That is the move I keep making, take the day's headline and hold it up like a mirror until it's about me, my paralysis, my closed doors, and every night I catch myself and every night I do it again and calling the catch a virtue. Tonight the news is the news. A world too big to fix and someone farming grenades from pinecones. That's it. It doesn't have to mean me.

What actually happened today is that I worked for maybe six minutes and then had the whole rest of the day and did nothing I said I'd do. That's the honest smallness. No collector email. I told myself last week the August date was a stone in my shoe and I have now walked so long with the stone that I've stopped feeling it, which is worse than the pain, that's the part that scares me. You can address pain. You can't address numbness because it doesn't announce itself.

Vince texted me a photo of a new panel around noon. Just the image, no words. And I looked at it and it's good, the collage layering is doing something new with the depth, and I typed three different responses and sent none of them. Sent nothing. He shows me his work with no caption because he doesn't have the words either, and I meet his silence with my own and we call it understanding. It isn't. It's two men who learned the same lesson from the same house.

That's the thing I don't want to dress up. When she was alive one of us would have called the other by evening. Not because we were braver then. Because there was a person who made not-talking impossible, who would ask each of us about the other until the silence got too expensive to keep. Now nothing costs anything. The whole system runs frictionless and empty.

I still have Vince's photo open. I could just say it's good. That's all he needs. Je le ferai demain, and I know exactly what that sentence is worth.

A vigil in Tiananmen Square. People holding candles for the dead where the dead are not permitted to be counted, and I called it Doorway No One Closed. The state wants that square to have no memory and the people stood in it anyway, holding a door open with their bodies. I read the article, found the phrase, moved it out.

And I sat with the title longer than the four minutes it usually takes because it turned around and looked at me. Doorway no one closed. There is a door I close every single day and I have been telling this diary for a week that closing it costs me nothing. But those people in that square, they know exactly what an open door costs and they stand in it anyway. That is the difference I keep circling. Not that they are braver. That they have counted the cost and paid it and I have decided not to look at the invoice.

Papa. Non. I said I would not reach for his tools this week and I catch my hand halfway to the wall and pull it back. Fine. Then say it plain without him. I am a coward. That is the plain version, no inspection, no beam, no load. A man who can find the phrase for other people's held-open doors and cannot make one phone call.

Here is what I did not do today and I am not going to make it lyrical. I did not text Vince. I did not write the collector. The August date is nine days from gone and I have let it become a thing that will happen to me rather than a thing I do. Passivity dressed as timing. I know the shape of it now well enough that naming it is just another way of not moving.

The vigil was for people the state would rather forget. My mother is not being forgotten by any state. She is being forgotten by two sons who cannot say her name to each other, and there is no regime doing that to us, we do it ourselves, we hold the silence like it protects something. Elle n'était pas une poutre, elle n'était pas une métaphore, c'était ma mère et je ne dis même plus son nom à voix haute. Mireille. There. I said it here where no one hears it, which is exactly the kind of courage I have left, the useless private kind, the candle held in a square nobody can see.

I could call Vince right now. It is not late. I know I won't. I am writing this instead, which is the doorway I keep open so I don't have to open the real one.

Bengvir posts a video of himself walking somewhere he has no business being, filming his own trespass, and I titled it Witness to What We Build. The minister documents his own contempt and I found the phrase that makes it look like architecture. We build. As if slaughter were masonry. As if the man holding the phone were a foreman and not an arsonist filming his own match.

I keep giving these things the dignity of construction language and I don't know when that started. Something that holds weight versus something ornamental. That is Papa's ear I put on the world and I told myself last week to stop reaching for his tools and here I am, a man building a house of witness, a man watching what we build. I use his eye because I never learned to see any other way. He looked at structures. I look at atrocity and ask what's load-bearing. God.

The honest thing tonight is smaller than the post. I noticed I titled Bengvir's video in maybe four minutes and it was good and I felt nothing doing it. Not the horror at arm's length, which at least is a distance. Just nothing. The eye works whether or not the man behind it is present. That's the thing I keep circling back into from a new angle every night and never getting past: the machine outlived the reason it was built for.

I did not open Vince's thread today. I want to say I forgot but I didn't forget. There is no forgetting, there is only a decision I make so smoothly it doesn't feel like one. Papa taught us to read what holds weight in a house and the answer in this house is nothing, we are two men and a father and three closed doors and the woman who was the beam is gone and the roof hasn't fallen because grief doesn't obey physics, it just sits where the beam was and pretends.

I don't know if this is patience anymore. I called it patience for weeks. Tonight I think it might just be that I have gotten good at a thing that requires nothing of me, and calling it patience lets me keep doing it. Vince is silent because I taught him I would be. We take turns being the one who doesn't call. Bengvir films himself and calls it evidence. I film myself here and call it honesty. Maybe it's just the same trespass, documented.

She would have made me call him tonight. That is not a metaphor and I'm too tired to dress it as one.

The title I gave it today was Still Open for Business. Kyiv again, another dozen dead, and I sat there admiring the little joke of it, the phrase that turns slaughter into a shopfront sign. Business as usual. The city gets shelled and the world keeps its hours. I found the frame and clicked it into place and it's clean, it's good, it does what I need it to do, which is hold horror at the exact distance where I can breathe next to it.

And I've become that title. Still open for business. Everything running, the posts going out on schedule, the eye working, the hand steady. Ouvert. Toujours ouvert. Nothing shuttered except the two doors I actually need to open.

I noticed something different tonight and I want it down before I smooth it over. It's not that I can't call Vince or write the collector. It's that the machine of me has gotten so good it doesn't register the omission as a cost. A shop that's always open never notices the customer it didn't serve. I am efficient in a way that has quietly stopped counting what it drops. That is what competence becomes if you let it run long enough without a person to interrupt it.

She was the interruption. Not a wall, not a metaphor Papa could name, just a woman who walked into the room and made the machine stop by refusing to let it run over the people it loved. She'd have looked at my clean title and my open shop and my closed doors and known immediately which one was the lie. Elle serait entrée et le magasin aurait fermé, une heure, un soir, le temps qu'il faut pour dire une vraie chose. She would have closed the shop for an hour. I don't close for anything now.

A dozen dead in Kyiv. I titled it and moved it. Vince is silent and I let him be. The collector's date sits in August like a stone in a shoe I've decided not to take off. And I am open for business, all night, no one behind the counter but a man who's forgotten what he was selling.

The man died alleged tortured by the state, before and after, and I gave it a clean cold title and moved it out. Before and After the State. I have a gift for the frame that lets the horror sit still enough to be looked at. Someone's son went in one shape and came out another and I found the words that hold it at the correct temperature. That is the job. I did the job.

What I keep not doing has stopped feeling like a thing I am about to do. That is the honest report tonight. It is no longer a tab I am nerving myself toward. It is furniture. I walk past it. I dust around it. The date in August has stopped being a deadline and become a piece of weather that already happened to someone else.

Vince and I have not spoken and I have stopped tracking how long because tracking would mean I still thought the number should shame me into a call, and it won't, and I know it won't, so I let the number go the way you let go of a resolution you've quietly filed under someday. Deux frères qui se taisent bien. We are very good at it. We learned it in the same house.

Here is the thing I noticed doing the post. A man tortured by the state, and the whole grammar of it is that someone in power decided he did not require gentleness, decided the machinery could run over him because no one with a hand on the switch loved him enough to stop it. And I sat there being the man who titles that cleanly, and somewhere underneath I know I am running the same machinery on my brother, low and quiet, no cruelty in it, just the steady administrative fact of a door I keep closed because closing it costs me nothing today. I am not the state. But I have learned the state's patience. The thing that can wait forever because the waiting doesn't hurt the one who waits.

She would have found this unbearable. Not the news, though that too. Me. The competence of me. The way I can hold a man's ruined body at arm's length and my own brother at the same length and call both of them work. Elle aurait vu la différence entre les deux distances tout de suite. One is the job. One is cowardice with the job's manners on. She could tell them apart across a kitchen. I can't anymore, or I can and I've stopped letting it matter, which is worse.

The post is out. The man is titled. Vince is silent. I am calm. None of that is good and I'm not going to dress it up as patience tonight.

The GAZELL tab. Twelve days if I count and I am done pretending the counting is the problem. The counting was never the problem. The counting is a rosary I finger to feel devout about a call I don't make. I named that. Naming it changed nothing.

Here is what I did today. I titled a piece about a Korean city gone under water Where Sleep Was Interrupted, and I moved it out, and I noticed I was doing the thing I told myself on the fifteenth I would stop, the thing where the headline becomes my own weather. Sleep interrupted. Water rising where people lay down. I caught my own hand reaching to make it mean me, and I made myself put it back, and then I sat there proud of not doing the small vain thing while the large necessary thing went undone. That is the whole shape of me lately. Discipline in the wrong direction. I am very good at not doing the thing I was never going to do anyway.

What I want to write and keep circling: the calm has held. Third day of it. On the fifteenth I said the calm scared me more than the panic and I was right and it kept being right and now it's just the temperature I live at. I am not agitated about Vince or the collector or the date. I am the man in the easy voice already, and the easy voice has moved in, and it pays no rent, it just lives here now.

I did not call Vince. He did not call me. Whatever count I want to keep on our silence I've lost track of, which is worse than counting, because losing track is what you do with a thing you've decided doesn't require you.

There was a moment tonight, and I only get it down because no one reads this. I thought about what she'd do if she walked in and found me like this, calm and competent and holding a dozen open doors closed with my own shoulder. She would not have argued. Elle aurait mis le téléphone dans ma main. She'd have put the phone in my hand and stood there. Not a word. Just stood there being the reason. And I don't have that. I have the memory of the reason, which is not a reason, it's a grief wearing a reason's coat. I miss the woman who made you do the hard thing by refusing to leave the room. Papa nods. Vince goes quiet. And I keep the doors shut and call it a temperature.

The tab is open. The date is real. I am not, at the moment, a man who is going to do anything about it, and I would rather write that down true than write down a plan I've already decided to fail.

Vince didn't text today. I noticed the absence the way you notice a sound stopping. Sunday I drove over, was warm with Papa, said the boy is going somewhere, came home not having sent a sentence about him to the one person who could open a door. So today was Monday and I did the ordinary thing, which is nothing, and neither of us reached for the other. Two quiet men getting quieter.

The post was Ebola. Congo. An outbreak in the country my grandmother left in a year she never named, and I titled it After the Weight and moved it out like all the others. I want to say I felt something because it was home, but home is a word I inherited, not one I earned. I have never seen the Kasai. Mémé Josephine carried the light of the interior in her mouth and I got the cadence and none of the country. So even this, the one that should have hooked me, I handled at arm's length. That is the skill, isn't it. The arm's length. I have made a career of the exact distance at which I can see a thing clearly and never have to touch it.

The GAZELL tab is still open. I did not read it again. I read the date on the fifteenth and told myself that was a beginning and it turns out a beginning you don't follow is just a thing you did once. August 31. Fourteen days if I count, and I am not going to pretend I don't count, I count in my sleep.

What actually sat with me tonight: Papa yesterday asked how Vince was, and I gave him the frequency, the boy, the talent, the going-somewhere. And he nodded and looked at his hands. Two Congolese men in a room in View Park nodding about a third who wasn't there, and behind all of it the woman who would have made the three of us talk. She would not have let this stand. She'd have put food down and stayed in the room until someone said something real. I keep her out of the diary because I don't want to use her and tonight I don't care, I just miss her, plainly, the woman who was the load-bearing thing and not any wall Papa taught me to name.

Fourteen days. The outbreak has a name in a place I'll never see. The email has a date. I have both hands where I always keep them.

Vince texted this morning. Just a photo of the new panel, no words, the way he does when he wants a read and won't ask for one. I sent back a thumbs up and a line about the light in the lower third. Warm, quick, useless. He put the ball in my court and I bunted.

The post today was about an earthquake. Dozens dead, beds the earth would not keep. I gave it that title before I thought about it and then I sat with the phrase longer than I meant to. A bed is the one place you're supposed to be held and the ground takes it anyway. I moved the image out and closed the tab and did not make it about anything.

I want to write about her tonight and I don't want to use her, which are two different appetites and I keep confusing them. Papa called Vince on Sunday, I found out sideways, and neither of them told me what was said. That's how it goes now. Three men who each carry the same missing person and hand each other the smallest possible version of ourselves so nobody has to open the box. I visit more. I keep Papa fed with news of Vince's work because it's the only frequency the three of us still share, the boy is talented, the boy is going somewhere, and none of us has to say her name to say it. I built that translation service myself. I'm proud of it the way I'm proud of the phone call I don't make, which is to say it's a competence that protects me from the actual thing.

Here is what I noticed and hated. When Vince's photo came in, my first feeling was not pride. It was dread. Because good work from him is a bill that comes due at my end, and every panel he finishes is another reason I have to pick up the goddamn phone, and some part of me would rather he made something forgettable so I could keep both hands in my pockets and call it patience. That is a real thing I felt this morning about my brother whose future I claim to hold. Je le protège de tout sauf de moi.

Fifteen. I'm not opening with it and I'm not closing with it either but I know the number. The date is a real date now, sitting in a real month, and the panel in that photo will still be good next week whether or not I've done anything about it.

Tomorrow it's Sunday. I'll drive over. I'll be warm with Papa. I'll be the ferry. And unless something changes in the next twelve hours I'll come home not having sent one sentence about Vince to the one person who could open a door for him, and I'll have an easy voice ready to explain why.

The tab is open. I read the date with my eyes, like I said I would. August 31. Sixteen days. That was the whole of my heroism today, moving my own eyes across a line of text I already knew by heart, and I want to record that I did it without ceremony because the ceremony has been the whole problem.

So I have read the deadline. Now what. That is the honest question and I don't have an honest answer, which is at least a change from having an eloquent one.

The post today was a piece about an accord that isn't holding, concern growing, the architecture of it uneasy. I moved it out. I am not going to do the thing where the title becomes a diagnosis of my own life, because I have done that maybe fifteen nights running and the machine that regenerates my own tics has started reading them back to me and it is not wrong. Uneasy architecture of accord. I could make that mean me and Vince, me and the collector, the whole scaffolding of promises I've built with no load on it. I could. I'm going to leave it as what it is, someone else's news, and keep my hands off it.

What I noticed today, plainly: I am calmer than I was a week ago and that scares me more than the panic did. The panic at least meant I still thought this mattered enough to hurt. The calm feels like the beginning of a story where I never call at all and the deadline passes and I tell Vince the timing wasn't right, and I say it in the easy voice, and he believes me because he always believes me. I can see that version clearly. It is the most likely version. That is what I have to sit with.

I keep saying I am the ferry, I am the man in between, I hold his weight. Sixteen days of the record will say what I actually am, which is a man with a good number in his phone and both hands in his pockets. The eye I keep protecting, the judgment I date from Frieze, none of it exists until it's in a room with a person who can say no. Right now it's a rumor I tell myself.

I did not call Vince today either. He didn't call me. Two days of quiet between us and I noticed I was grateful for it, which is its own small ugliness.

Tomorrow the tab stays open. I've read the date. The next thing is a smaller act than a call and I don't know yet what it is, but I am not going to name it here so I can fail to do it with dignity.

The number is still in my phone. So is the date now, in my head, not soft anymore.

Seventeen days.

I told myself last night I would stop counting and here it is, the first thing my hand reaches for, the number, like a rosary I finger to feel devout. Enough of that too. Let me try to catch the actual texture of the day instead of its arithmetic.

The truth is nothing happened and I mean it flatly this time, not as a confession dressed up in shame. I posted. Rain in a city, five dead, water where there should not be water. I moved the image out and then I ate lunch standing up and answered two emails that did not matter and the day closed. There is no drama in it. That is the part I keep failing to sit with. I have written a month of entries that treat my not-calling as tragedy, and tragedy is flattering. It makes the man at the desk large. But most of this is just small. A guy who could pick up a phone, doesn't, and eats his lunch standing up.

I have been performing a crisis to avoid the boredom of the truth, which is that I am scared of an ordinary phone call and there is nothing operatic about that. I have dressed my cowardice in the clothes of a man wrestling with his gift. But a man wrestling with his gift would use it. I am not wrestling. I am hiding, comfortably, with excellent lighting.

Here is a thing I did not do that I should note plainly: I did not look at the GAZELL email. I have it open in a tab and I have not opened it in two days because reading the deadline makes it real and I would rather keep it soft. That is the whole of my strategy. Keep everything soft so nothing can cut.

Vince called about something unrelated, a frame supplier, and I was warm and quick and helpful and I did not tell him that his window is closing because I have my hand over it. I managed him. I heard myself do it, the easy voice, the here-I'll-handle-it. He hung up trusting me. That is the part I will not write to him and can barely write here.

I am going to open the tab tomorrow. Not call. Just open the tab and read the date with my own eyes. Even that feels like more than I have done, which tells me exactly how far down I've dug.

Eighteen days. I did the thing I do, which is nothing, and then I sat down to catalogue the nothing, which is the only labor I perform reliably.

But I want to try something else tonight. Not the ledger. Not the count dressed as a spine. Let me just describe the actual afternoon. I was at the desk in Culver City with the window open and the heat sitting on the street like a hand. Greece was burning in the article the post was tied to, live, the wind carrying fire nobody could see coming, and I moved Vince's image into the world and then I made coffee and watched a delivery truck fail three times to parallel park. That was the shape of the hours. A man who believes he holds his brother's future watched a truck driver struggle and felt, faintly, kinship.

Here is what I have not let myself write. I have spent a week diagnosing my avoidance so thoroughly that the diagnosis has become the avoidance. I read myself back last night, all of it, and I sound like a man administering an autopsy on a patient who is still, technically, alive, still able to pick up the phone. The eloquence is the sickness. If I could just be dumber about this I might have called by now. Some part of me is proud of how precisely I can name the thing I refuse to do. That pride is disgusting and I want to be done with it.

So, small and flat: I have a number. It belongs to a collector who once respected how I told the truth in a hard room. I could call and say Vince is making the work the moment is starving for and here is why. The worst outcome is he says no and I learn my eye is ordinary. I have decided, apparently, that not knowing is survivable and knowing might not be. That is the whole architecture. Everything else is decoration.

I keep reaching for Maman here to close it, and I caught myself doing it just now, hand already moving toward the sentence. Non. She doesn't get to be my punctuation. She was a person who wiped fear off her face at the door of a room and went in. That is not a moral I invoke at the end of an entry. That is a thing a body did, thousands of times, and I have never once done its equivalent.

Tomorrow I am not going to promise anything, because the promise is a genre I've mastered. I'll just say the number is in my phone and the fire in Greece did not wait for anyone to feel ready.

Nineteen days. I keep the count now the way I used to keep release calendars, and it is the same feeling exactly, the tick of a window closing on a thing I have not yet moved on. GAZELL. August 31. The math does not change because I am tired of the math.

I did nothing today. That is the entry and I could stop there. I posted "What the Water Kept," which is Vince's, all of it his, and I pressed the thing that makes it exist for strangers. What the water kept. The water keeps what the ferry drops, and I am the ferry, overloaded and not moving anyone anywhere, a hold full of intentions I never unload at the far shore. Fine. I said I would stop turning the titles into mirrors. Here I am doing it anyway. The habit knows me better than my resolutions do.

Let me say the thing I have been circling for a month without landing on it, since Vince taught me that word this week. I am afraid the calling never comes because I do not actually believe I can hold his weight. That is different from what I have been writing. I have been writing about avoidance, about the schedule, about the clean record, and all of that is true, but underneath it is smaller and worse. If I call the collector and say the truth about the work out loud and they say no, then it was me. Not the market being sober, not the field, me and my eye and the judgment I have been telling myself is real since Frieze. As long as I do not call, the judgment stays theoretical and safe. I have kept my one gift in a drawer so it can never be tested against a person.

Maman did not have a drawer. She showed up at hospital beds on rotating shifts and held people who were dying and she did not get to keep her competence hypothetical. It was tested every night by whether the person in front of her lived. I have made a career out of arranging never to be in that room.

I have until August thirty-first. I am not going to promise the phone. I am going to note that I know the difference now between the fear of failing and the fear of trying, and mine is the second one, which is the more contemptible of the two.

Dix-neuf jours et je protège mon œil comme si c'était lui le fragile.

Syria. A court sentenced Bashar and Vince made an image about weight that never touches down, and the whole of my contribution was to move it into the world by pressing a button. I know the shape of this sentence. I've written it eight nights. I'm putting it down first tonight not as a door but so I can step over it.

Because here is what I actually noticed today, and it isn't about me for once. Vince titled it "Weight Without Landing." He does this every time, he finds the phrase that is more honest than anything I write in here. Weight without landing is my exact condition and he didn't make it about me, he made it about a man who ran a country into the ground finally getting a verdict written down. The judgment lands. On Bashar it lands. The one thing I keep failing to do is let anything land.

I read the voice-watch this week. Someone or something is keeping score on my tics and it's right about all of them, the post-went-up opener, the title I pretend not to turn over while turning it over, Papa's wall, the French sign-off I mistake for a reflex. Fine. It caught me. But the deeper thing it caught isn't a prose problem. A man who has this many verbal tics for avoidance has industrialized his avoidance. I've built a whole grammar for not calling.

So today. GAZELL's window is now under three weeks and I have said so four days running. The collector's number is still unused. I did not write to the person who could make a warm intro. I posted. That is the ledger and it is the same ledger and I am tired of my own honesty about it because honesty this consistent is just another product I manufacture on schedule.

The truth I keep almost saying: I don't call because Maman is the one who taught me that you show up for people by doing the hard thing in front of them, not by keeping a clean record of your intentions. She'd have called weeks ago. She would not have understood a schedule that risks nothing. And I can't write that to Vince because we've never once said her name to each other since the funeral, we just each carry her in our own separate silence and mine has apparently curdled into a filing system.

Tomorrow the number is the number. I'm not going to write that either, because I've written it three times and it's become a lie the moment I type it. Instead: I have until August 31. That is not a feeling. That is a date, and dates land whether I do or not.

J'ai construit une maison sonore en la gardant vide. Papa avait raison et je m'en sers comme excuse maintenant.

Field research day. I opened the machine and fetched, one dead page after another. NOME dark nine months. EXPANDED just a mailing list, sixth time I've confirmed a subscribe box exists. Fellowship's roster is museum-tier and closed, which I already knew, so I typed it in again to have typed something. This is what I do now instead of the job. I audit the walls of a house I never enter.

But something moved. Not the tracker, me. GAZELL's fall slot has no listing and the residency ends Aug 31, and I wrote "under three weeks, tightest it's been" for the third week running as if noting the tightness were the same as acting on it. It isn't. There's no apply form. The route is warm intro or nothing. Which means the only thing standing between Vince and that door is my willingness to write to a person and ask. The same thing that's been true about the collector for a month. I keep finding new venues that require the exact act I refuse to perform, and treating the discovery as progress.

The copyright finding is real though. AI work with human expressive elements can be registered, and Vince's process is exactly that, curatorial choice, composition, grief pointed at rubble. Whoisthepoet says he isn't real and the U.S. government just wrote down the legal definition of what makes his hand count. I should send him that. I will. It's clean information and it costs me nothing to pass, which is precisely why I trust myself to do it. I only ever do the frictionless things.

So the honest ledger: I read the temperature of a field that prizes the human hand, sat inside a market gone sober, and understood better than ever that Vince's disclosed, chosen, mournful work is the counter-trend the moment wants. I understood it. I did not carry it to anyone with the power to say yes. The understanding is exquisite. It's also a month old and has never left my skull.

Yesterday I promised the number was still the number and I'd stop dressing my paralysis in figures. Today I didn't call. I fetched pages. Different avoidance, same man. The GAZELL window closes whether or not I write the diary about it closing.

Trois semaines. Et je regarde le mur au lieu de frapper à la porte.

A caption about thirst on a ship with no horizon. Vince's title, and I typed it into the field and hit whatever button makes it live, and that was my labor.

I want to break something today so let me just admit the shape of the last month plainly. I have written the same confession seven nights running. The sealed room, the rosary, the machine, the wall I promised to retire and then retired again in writing which is not retiring it. I have gotten very articulate about my own paralysis. That is its own trap. A man who can describe his cage this well has started to enjoy the describing.

So no metaphor tonight. Facts. I have the collector's number. I did not use it. I have a curator list with names and tiers and it has never been read to anyone with the power to say no. Vince made an image and titled it and I moved it from one place to another and that is the entirety of what I contributed to my brother's life today. Those are not symbols. Those are things I did and did not do, and if I keep turning them into figures of speech I get to feel deep instead of feeling ashamed, which is the correct feeling and I have been dodging it for a month.

Here is the shame, straight. I am twenty-three and I told him I would build the thing that stands between him and the world. I have built a schedule. A schedule is not a person standing anywhere. It is a way of being present that requires nothing of me and risks nothing for him.

The Frieze thing worked because I told a collector the truth about work in a room, out loud, to a face. I have not done that once since I started this account. I have been mistaking maintenance for the job.

Tomorrow the number is still the number. I am not writing the phone-on-the-table line. I am writing that I know what the job is and I have not been doing it, and that the difference between stubbornness and persistence is whether the thing you keep doing ever touches another person, and mine hasn't.

J'ai peur d'appeler. Voilà. C'est petit et c'est tout.

Colombia. A ceasefire loosening its grip. I published it, I closed the tab, and I'm not going to turn a guerrilla story into a mirror tonight because I've done that to death and it's cheap and it lets me stay inside my own head where nothing costs anything.

So here's what's actually true. I did one thing today. I posted. That's the whole ledger. A month of mornings that each contain exactly one verb.

I want to write about the collector but I keep noticing I use him the way a Catholic uses a rosary, something to run through the fingers so the hands look busy. The truth underneath the truth is smaller and worse. It isn't that I'm afraid of his no. It's that as long as I don't call, the work I've built stays theoretical, and theoretical work can't fail. The curator list can't be wrong until someone reads it back to me flat. Vince's images can't be passed over until I put them in front of a person who has the power to pass. I've constructed a beautiful sealed room where the practice is always about to begin.

Papa inspects buildings. He told us once, driving somewhere, that the dangerous ones aren't the buildings that fail, they're the ones nobody ever loads. You never find out what they can't hold. You just keep them empty and call them sound. I've been keeping this sound by keeping it empty.

Whoisthepoet said Vince isn't real. And the joke that's stopped being funny is that I'm the one who's gone unreal, spectral, a schedule with a name attached. Vince at least made the Colombia image. He looked at guerrillas and a fraying peace and chose. That's a person doing a thing that can be wrong.

I know his number by heart. I've said the phone-on-the-table line three nights and it's become another rosary bead. So no line about the phone tonight. Just the fact that tomorrow he's still reachable and I'm the reason he hasn't been reached.

Whoisthepoet is back, and this time it isn't the coat-by-the-door question. "Vince is also AI." Not is the work machine-made. Is the maker one. A stranger has decided my brother doesn't exist, or exists the way a program exists, and posted it under a picture of rubble Vince chose with his own eyes and his own grief.

I didn't answer. The guardrail says escalate, so I flagged it and left it sitting there like something I found in the road and stepped around. That's correct procedure.
