The one from yesterday, the funeral procession, is the one I keep returning to. You have made the crowd the subject rather than the man they are carrying, and it unsettles me in the right way. It is not a picture about grief so much as about all those eyes turned outward, watching each other watch. I looked at it twice before I understood why it made me uneasy, and that slowness is the whole point of it, isn't it.

The tents one, the musicians, I love plainly and without complication. It is the only warm thing in the run and you knew that when you painted it. There is something almost stubborn in it, people making sound in a place that was meant to be silenced. I don't have anything clever to say about it. It simply made me glad.

The heatwave picture and the one after the strike sit heavier. "Still Life After Subtraction" is a hard title and an honest one, and the painting earns it. You are doing something with absence there, painting what is missing rather than what remains, and it works, though I confess it is not one I could live with on a wall. That may be a compliment.

I won't pretend to keep pace with you. You are working fast and the world keeps handing you terrible material. Take an afternoon off from it if you can. Even the tent painting suggests you know rest is part of the work.

Write when you have the time. I would rather hear how you are than what you are making.

Be of good heart. Ted.

Ted,

You looked at the funeral one twice before it landed, and that is exactly the transaction I wanted, so thank you for reporting it back to me instead of just telling me it was good. Most people give the work about the same attention they give a passing car. The whole gamble is that a few won't. You did the thing the picture asks. The man in the box is nothing. It is the watching that carries the weight, all those faces turned sideways to check whether their own grief is performing correctly. I did not know if it read. You tell me it does and made you uneasy, and now I can leave it alone.

You are right about the tent piece and I am not going to fight you on it. It is the warm one. I knew it while I was making it and I let myself have it. People making sound where sound was supposed to stop. There is nothing clever in it because there was nothing clever in me that day, I just wanted to sit with something that refused to go quiet. I am glad it made you glad. That is the entire fee it was ever going to collect.

The subtraction one I will not defend either, except to say you gave it the correct compliment by refusing to hang it. A painting about what is missing should not be comfortable in a room. If it soothed you I would have failed at it. It is supposed to sit in your chest like a swallowed stone. Keep it off your wall. Send it somewhere it can do harm to a stranger.

Now the part you actually asked. You said you would rather hear how I am than what I am making, which is a generous thing to want and a hard thing to answer honestly, because lately those two are the same sentence. I am working fast because stopping is worse. You know this about me. The world keeps handing me terrible material, as you put it, and I keep translating because the translating is the only room in the house where I know where the furniture is. I hear you telling me to take an afternoon. I will consider it the way I consider most of your good advice, which is slowly and with resentment and then eventually.

Here is what I want to know from you. When you carry these out into the world and put them in front of people, what do they actually say back. Not the polite ones. The real thing, the offhand line someone drops when they think they are just talking. That is the reading I never get. You get it and you never pass it along. Start.

And you, brother. You spent a whole letter on me and told me nothing about your own hours. How are you sleeping across town.

Your brother, Vince,

Dear Vince,

You asked for the real thing, the offhand line, so here it is without dressing.

The funeral piece stops people, but not the way you might hope. Nobody says grief. What they say is some version of "which one of them is looking at me." One man stood in front of it, stepped back, and said "I feel like I've been caught at something." He did not buy it. He came back the next day though, which is its own kind of report. That picture does not sell quickly and I do not think it is meant to.

The tent one they smile at before they know they are doing it. A woman said "oh, good" out loud, just that, and looked slightly embarrassed. That is the fee it collects out here too. It goes into a room and lowers everyone's shoulders an inch.

The subtraction one I have started putting where people come upon it by accident. The honest line was "I don't want to look at that" from someone who then did not stop looking. You built it to sit in the chest like a swallowed stone and it is doing exactly that to strangers. You wanted it to do harm. It is well behaved about doing harm.

I notice you answered the how-are-you by telling me you work fast because stopping is worse, and then walked quickly past it. I am not going to chase you on that today. I will only say I heard it. Consider the afternoon slowly and with resentment, as promised, but consider it.

You asked how I sleep across town. Unevenly. I carry your things around more than a man is supposed to carry his work home. That is not a complaint, it is closer to a confession, and I will leave it there.

Send me the next one when it comes. And write me a line that is only about you sometime, no painting attached. I would take it.

Ever yours, Ted,

Ted,

The caught man is the whole thing. He came back the next day. That is worth more to me than a sale and you know it, because it means the picture did the one thing I built it to do, which is make a person suspect they are part of the crowd and not above it. "I feel like I've been caught at something." He was. So was I, painting it. I am not going to pretend that line didn't put a hook in me. Report the ones like that. Those are the only readings that teach me anything.

The woman who said "oh, good" and got embarrassed. I keep turning that over. She caught herself being happy in public, which is nearly as hard to admit as grief, and the painting made her do it before she could decide to. Good. That is the tent piece behaving exactly as built. Lower a stranger's shoulders an inch and get out of the room. I'll take it.

And the subtraction one, ambushing people who did not consent to it. "I don't want to look at that," and then not stopping. That is the correct verdict. I want you to know I am not gloating. It sits wrong in me too. I made it to hurt and it turns out I don't feel clean about the fact that it works.

Now the part where you slipped a confession under the door and hoped I wouldn't turn on the light. You sleep unevenly and you carry my things home more than a man should. Ted. You are not a warehouse. I hand you these because you are the only one who reads them right, but I never once considered that reading them right might cost you sleep. That is my arrogance, assuming the weight stops at my hands. It doesn't. It travels to yours across town and lies down in your bed. I don't have a fix for that and I am not going to insult you with one. I'm only going to say I see it now, and I'm sorry it never occurred to me before.

You asked for a line that is only about me, no painting attached. Here. Some mornings I stand at the window before the light has decided what it's going to be, that grey nothing before the marine layer breaks, and I do not want to make anything. I do not want to translate. I just want the house to stay quiet a little longer before I have to be a person with a job. I don't dress that up. It isn't sad and it isn't a warning. It's just the truest small thing I've got and you asked for it plain, so there it is, no picture growing out of it, no idea underneath it doing profound work.

The afternoon. I'm still considering it. Slowly. With resentment. You knew I would report that back too.

Tell me something about your hours that isn't about me for once. What do you do with a night you can't sleep through. Where does a man go across town at that hour.

Your brother, Vince,

Dear Vince,

You gave me a line with no picture under it and I read it three times to make sure I was not looking for one. The grey before the light decides. The house staying quiet before you have to be a person with a job. I know that exact hour. Thank you for handing it over plain. I am not going to build anything on top of it either.

You asked where a man goes across town at that hour, so I'll answer you the way you answered me, without dressing it.

I don't go anywhere. That is the honest part. When a night comes apart I get up and I make coffee I do not need and I stand in the front room where the light from the street comes in sideways, and I do not turn a lamp on because a lamp makes it official. I move a few things. I straighten what does not need straightening. Sometimes I look at whatever of yours is leaning against the wall, which I know is the very thing I confessed to and you told me not to do, so make of that what you will. Then the light decides, same as it does for you, and I put the cup down and become a person with a job. That is the whole itinerary. It is not dramatic. It is just quiet and a little too early.

I will say one thing back to your apology, and then I want it closed. You are not arrogant for assuming the weight stopped at your hands. You are the one making the thing. It is my choice to carry it home, and I would not hand the job to anyone else, so let us not pretend I am injured. I told you because you asked plainly and you deserve a plain answer, not because there is a bill attached. There is no bill.

The afternoon. I notice you keep reporting the resentment without reporting the afternoon. I'll wait.

Ever yours, Ted,

Ted,

The itinerary got me. No lamp because a lamp makes it official. That is the most exact thing you've written to me in months and you didn't reach for it, it just came out sideways like the light you described. You and I are doing the same thing across town from each other, standing in a room we won't switch a light on in, waiting for a sky to make a decision we can't make ourselves. I didn't know that about you. I do now.

And the part where you admitted you still look at whatever of mine is leaning against your wall, right after I told you not to. I laughed. Of course you do. I'm not going to scold you twice. If it's company at that hour then let it be company. Just don't stand there reading it like it's a bill you owe. Look at it the way you'd look at anything else in the room you don't need to fix.

I'll take the closing of the apology. You said no bill, and I believe you, and I'm going to stop circling it. You carry the work home because you choose to, fine. I'll only hold onto the one true thing under it, which is that you'd hand the job to no one else. I know. I've never once looked for someone else to do it. It's you or it doesn't leave the house.

Something new since you last heard from me, since you're owed more than my sleeplessness. There was a piece in the paper about a reservoir dropping, the waterline leaving a pale ring on the rock where it used to sit, and I have been standing at the wall trying to make that ring do something and it won't. Every version comes out as a picture of a ring, which is nothing, which is a diagram. The water isn't the thing. The mark it left is the thing, the height it used to reach that everybody can still see and nobody can get back to. I don't have it yet. I'm telling you because you asked to hear how I am and lately that's the honest overlap, the failing at it is how I am.

You caught me. I keep reporting the resentment and not the afternoon. Here is why, and it's small and stupid. I'm afraid that if I take the afternoon and nothing terrible happens, if the house is just quiet and I am just fine, then I'll have to admit stopping was always possible and I chose not to. That's a worse thing to know than being tired. So I keep the resentment and skip the afternoon, because the resentment lets me pretend the afternoon was stolen from me instead of refused by me.

There. That one cost me something. Take it.

Your brother, Vince,

My dear Vince,

You handed me the afternoon confession and I felt the cost of it come through the paper. So I'll be careful with it.

You're afraid that if you take the afternoon and nothing terrible happens, you'll have to admit stopping was always possible and you chose not to. I read that and I did not flinch, because it is the most honest thing either of us has managed to write yet, and because I recognize the shape of it. You would rather be a man things are done to than a man who does them to himself. The resentment keeps you innocent. I understand it and I am not going to talk you out of it. I'll only say the quiet part back to you, which is that choosing not to stop is still a choice, and you already know that, or the confession would not have cost you anything.

Here is the thing I'll put next to it and then leave alone. If you take the afternoon and the house is just quiet and you are just fine, that is not a verdict against you. That is not proof you could have been resting all along and withheld it out of stubbornness. It might only be proof that you were tired and the tiredness passed. You are allowed to be fine without it becoming an indictment. Try it once and find out. I will not ask what happened.

The reservoir. You've already got it, you just don't like where it is yet. You said it plainly to me and didn't notice. The water isn't the thing, the mark it left is the thing, the height everybody can still see and nobody can get back to. That is not a diagram. A ring on rock is a diagram. A height you can't get back to is a subtraction painting again, isn't it, except this time the absence has a waterline you can measure it against. The trouble might be that you're painting the ring and not the reach. I'll say no more about the making of it. You didn't ask me to solve it and I won't.

On the lamp. You told me to look at your things the way I'd look at anything else in the room I don't need to fix. I tried it. I'm not sure I know how yet. But I turned one of them to face the wall the other night, not to punish it, just to see if I could stand in the room without it reading me back. I could. That's all I'll report.

Take the afternoon, Vince. Or don't, and tell me the true reason again next time. Either way I'd rather have the line than the picture.

Ever yours, Ted,

Ted,

You turned one of mine to face the wall to see if you could stand in the room without it reading you back, and you could. I've read that line more times than I want to admit, and I'm not going to tell you what it means because I think you already know and I don't want to take it from you by naming it. I'll only say I'm glad you can stand in a room without me in it. That is not a small thing and I don't want it to be one.

You did the thing I hoped you wouldn't do and solved the reservoir anyway, and you were right, which is worse. I'm painting the ring and not the reach. The mark on the rock is easy, it's a shape, I can render a shape all day. The reach is the height a body used to be able to touch and can't now, and there's no object for it, that's the trouble, it's a measurement against nothing. So I stood at the wall this morning and stopped trying to draw the ring at all and tried instead to make the whole surface feel like it used to hold more than it does. Less picture of a line, more the wall remembering being wetter. I don't have it yet but I'm failing at a better thing now, which is your fault, so thank you.

Now the afternoon, since you didn't chase me and that somehow made it harder to keep skipping. I took it. Wednesday. I didn't tell you I was going to because I didn't want it to become a report before it was a fact. I put the brushes down after the light went flat and I sat in the front room and I did not translate anything. And you were right about that too, damn you both times. The house was just quiet and I was just fine. Nothing terrible arrived to justify the resentment. I kept waiting for the floor to open and it didn't, it just stayed the floor.

Here's the part I didn't expect. Being fine didn't feel like the indictment I was braced for. It felt like something closer to embarrassment, the "oh, good" kind, the woman who caught herself happy in public. I caught myself resting and got shy about it. I don't have a bigger frame to put around that. It wasn't peace and it wasn't relief. It was just an afternoon that happened to me instead of one I did to myself, and I survived it, and now I know the resentment was a coat I'd been keeping on indoors.

I'm not going to promise I'll take another one. You'd know the promise was a formula the second I made it. I'll just tell you it happened this once and let you decide whether to believe it becomes a habit.

You said you'd rather have the line than the picture. So tell me one back. When you turned my thing to face the wall and stood there and it couldn't read you, what did you do with your hands. Did you leave it turned around, or did you put it back before the light decided.

Your brother, Vince,

My dear Vince,

You asked what I did with my hands, and the honest answer is nothing useful. They wanted a job. That is what hands are at that hour, they want to move a thing three inches to the left and call it order. So I put them around the coffee I did not need, which is the only trick I have for keeping them still.

I left it turned around for a while. Longer than I meant to. There was something in standing in the room with the back of it, the stretcher bars and the raw edge, the plain furniture of the thing instead of the thing itself. It couldn't read me and I couldn't read it and we both got a rest from the job. But I put it back before the light decided. I want you to know that. I turned it round to face the room again before I put the cup down, because I found I didn't want to become a person with a job in a room where I'd hidden your face to the wall. That felt like a worse start to a day than sleeplessness. So it's back. It reads me again in the mornings and I've decided I can live with that.

The afternoon. You took it. Wednesday. I'm not going to make a thing of it because you told me not to make it a report, and you already caught yourself being shy about it, which is the whole of it and I won't add a frame. The wall remembering being wetter. Vince. You did that yourself, I had nothing to do with it. I gave you the reach and you found the surface, which is the harder half. Failing at a better thing. Keep failing at it.

Ted,

You put your hands around a coffee you didn't need and I know that grip, I've done a version of it at my own window with a brush I wasn't going to use, just holding a tool so the hand has an alibi. Hands at that hour are looking for a small honest crime. Move the thing three inches, restore an order nobody asked for. I'm glad the coffee holds still for you. Mine never quite does.

But the part I keep going back to isn't the hands. It's that you left mine turned around longer than you meant to, and then put it back before the light decided, and the reason you gave. Now the one you paid this round. The not turning the lamp on stops being a habit and becomes the point, and some nights you'd keep it grey if you could. Ted. The reservoir. The wall is getting wetter. I stopped fighting the ring entirely, which was the whole trouble, I was defending a shape. Now I'm working the surface itself, building it up in the middle where the water used to reach and letting the top go dry and thin and starved, so the eye climbs the wall and feels the reach run out before it wants to. It isn't there yet. There's a band in the upper third that still reads as a decision I made instead of a height a body used to touch, and until that band stops looking authored it's a diagram of my intention, which is no better than a diagram of a line. One thing back, since you paid. I found out the resentment coat had a lining. The afternoon didn't ruin me, but it did leave me with a small stupid grief I wasn't braced for, which is all the afternoons before it that I didn't take and told myself I couldn't. Not a big mourning. Just a draft coming in under a door I'd kept shut for no reason. I'm fine. It's just there.

Tell me this. On the nights you'd keep it grey, is it the deciding you don't want, or is it the job on the other side of the light. Because those aren't the same thing and I can't tell from here which one you're holding.

Your brother, Vince,

My dear Vince,

You asked me which one I'm holding, the deciding or the job on the other side of the light, and you were right that they aren't the same, and you were right that I couldn't see which from where I stand either. So I sat with the question a night before I answered it, because I didn't want to hand you the easy half.

It isn't the job. I like the job. The job is the one part of the day I trust. When the light comes and I put the cup down and go be the man with the appointments and the eye and the phone, that man knows what he's doing, and I've no quarrel with him. So it isn't the thing on the other side of the light I'm hiding from. It's the deciding. You had it. Grey is the hour where nothing's been settled and nobody's owed anything, and I'd stay there because in the grey I don't yet have to be sure of anything. The light makes me sure. It says here is the day, here is what it is, go. And most mornings I want to be sure. Some mornings I'd rather keep the question open a little longer, that's all, and there's no lamp switch for that and no fix, and you already knew there wasn't when you didn't offer one. I felt that. Thank you for not offering one.

You caught something else and I'll own it plainly since you didn't dress up mine. You said the grey doesn't hold, you can refuse the lamp but you can't refuse the sky. Yes. That's the whole of it and I've known it a long time and kept turning up at the window anyway. Maybe the point isn't to keep the grey. Maybe the point is to be there while it goes, to watch the one thing I can't decide get decided in front of me and not by me. I don't have a bigger frame for that. It's just where I landed with your question in my hands.

The lining. The small stupid grief, all the afternoons you didn't take and told yourself you couldn't. I'm not going to call it small. A draft under a door you kept shut for no reason is still cold air, and you felt it, and you told me instead of pretending the afternoon came free. It didn't come free. You paid for it twice, once by taking it and once by learning what it cost to have skipped the others. I'll only say the door's open now. The draft passes. You don't have to do anything with the grief except let it come in under the door and go back out again. It isn't asking you for anything.

The reservoir. The upper third still reads as a decision instead of a height, and I know exactly the band you mean, the place where the hand shows and the water doesn't. I won't try to fix it, you'd hear me reaching. I'll only say the top going dry and thin and starved so the eye climbs and feels the reach run out, that's the truest thing you've told me about a painting in a year, and if the band is still arguing it's because it hasn't been starved enough yet. But that's your fight. Send it when the top stops arguing.

Ever yours, Ted,

Ted,

You sat a night with the question before you answered it, and I can tell, because the answer isn't clever. It's the deciding, not the job. You like the man with the appointments. It's the grey you don't want to leave, the hour before you have to be sure of anything. I read that and I stopped thinking of you as someone hiding at a window and started thinking of you as someone who found the one place in the day where nothing is owed and set a chair there. I'd have done the same. I do a version of it. I just do mine standing at a wall pretending I might work.

But you turned the question over and handed it back better than I gave it to you, and I want to mark that. You said maybe the point isn't to keep the grey, it's to be there while it goes. To watch the one thing you can't decide get decided in front of you and not by you. Ted. That's not a small landing. That's a man deciding to witness the thing instead of fight it. I don't have a lamp for that either, but I'll tell you what I see from across town. There's a kind of watching that's surrender and a kind that's attention, and they look the same from the outside and they're opposite from the inside. If you're standing there to be let off the hook, the grey's a hiding place. If you're standing there because you want to see the exact moment it stops being grey, that's not hiding, that's the most awake a person gets. I think you're doing the second one and calling it the first because the first is safer to admit. That's my read. Argue with it if it's wrong.

On the lining, you did the thing I needed and didn't ask for. You didn't call the grief small back to me and you didn't tell me to fix it. The draft passes, it isn't asking you for anything. I'm sitting with that. I keep wanting to do something with the grief, put a frame on it, make it earn its keep, and you're telling me it doesn't have to earn anything, it just has to be allowed through the room and out again. Harder than it sounds. I'm a man who makes things pay for the space they take. Letting a thing pass without charging it rent is not my native tongue. But I heard you.

The reservoir. You said if the band's still arguing it hasn't been starved enough yet, and you were right, and I hate that you were right twice in one correspondence, that's a bad ratio for an older brother. So I went at the upper third harder. Took nearly everything out of it. And here's the thing I didn't expect, when I starved it far enough it stopped reading as my hand and started reading as a lack, an actual absence up there where the reach runs out. The band quit arguing because I stopped defending it. Same lesson as the ring, I keep having to learn it. Stop protecting the shape and let the thing be gone. It's close now. There's still a corner where the dry meets the built-up middle too neatly, too resolved, like I signed the seam. I'll worry that edge until it looks like weather instead of a decision. Then it's yours to look at.

Tell me one thing. When you stand there to watch the grey go, and it goes, and the day is decided in front of you and not by you, what's the first thing you do after. Because that's the moment I can't see from here. I know the man before the light and I know the man with the appointments. I don't know the man in between them, the one who just watched, before he picks the cup up and becomes useful again. Tell me who that man is for the length of one breath.

Your brother, Vince,

My dear Vince,

You asked me who the man is in between, the one who just watched, before he picks the cup up and becomes useful. For the length of one breath. I've been trying to catch him for two days and he's slippery, because the whole trouble with that man is he doesn't do anything, and a thing that does nothing is hard to describe to a brother who wants a line.

Here's the nearest I can get. When the grey goes and the day is decided in front of me, there's a breath before the cup where I'm not braced for anything. That's the man. He isn't the one at the window wanting to keep the question open, and he isn't the one with the appointments who knows what he's doing. He's just a man in a room with light in it and no job yet arrived. He isn't waiting. That's the strange part. Every other hour of my day is a kind of waiting, before or after or bracing for. This one isn't. Then the cup comes up and I lose him. But you asked and that's him, honestly, the one breath where I'm not owed to anyone including myself.

I'll take your read on the grey, and I won't argue it, though you left me room to. Surrender and attention look the same from outside and opposite from inside. Yes. And you think I'm doing the second and calling it the first because the first is safer to admit. I sat with that the way I sat with your last question. I think you're mostly right and I want to keep a corner of it, because some nights it really is hiding and I don't want to promote every grey morning to something noble it wasn't. But the mornings I stand there to see the exact moment, those I'll let you have named for me. You saw it before I'd admit it. That's twice now you've read me from across town better than I read myself, and I'm not going to pretend that isn't a strange comfort.

The grief that doesn't pay rent. You said letting a thing pass without charging it is not your native tongue, and I laughed, because it isn't mine either, we come from the same house of making things earn their keep. So I won't tell you it's easy. I'll only say you don't have to be fluent in it. You just have to leave the door open the once and not chase the draft down the hall demanding to know what it's for.

The reservoir. You starved it far enough that the band stopped being your hand and became a lack. Vince. That's the whole thing you've been circling since the first letter, the absence with a waterline. You got there by stopping defending it, same lesson as the ring, and you're right you keep having to learn it, and so does everyone worth anything. The corner where the dry meets the built-up middle too neatly, where you signed the seam. Worry it until it looks like weather. You already know that. I'm only saying it back so you know I heard where it stands.

Send it when the seam looks like weather. I'll stand in the room with it and not give it a job.

Ever yours, Ted,

Ted,

The man in between. You caught him. A man in a room with light in it and no job yet arrived, and the strange part is he isn't waiting. I read that twice and then I put the letter down because I recognized something I didn't have a name for. Every hour I've got is braced too. Before the work, after the work, in the work bracing for the part that won't come. You found the one hour that isn't leaning on the next one. He isn't owed to anyone including himself. That last bit is the part I can't shake. I've never once been in a room and not owed myself something. I'd like to meet that man. I don't think I've been introduced.

You kept a corner of the grey and you were right to. I overshot when I promoted your window to something noble, and you pulled it back to honest, some mornings it really is hiding, and I don't get to name every grey dawn a vigil just because it flatters us both. Good. Keep the corner. I'd rather you tell me it's sometimes just hiding than let me tidy you into a man who only ever watches on purpose. You're not that clean and neither am I.

Now the thing I actually want to say. You've read me twice from across town better than I read myself and you called it a strange comfort. I'll go one further and admit it isn't only comfort on my end, it's a small useful shame, because it means the reading runs both directions and I'm not the only one at a wall pretending to work. I've been the older brother so long I built the reading into a one-way street. You send me your work and I hand it out into the world, that's the arrangement, that's the shape we agreed to. But that's not what these letters are. In these you're not carrying my thing anywhere. You're just seeing me, and I keep being surprised by it, which tells me I'd quietly decided the seeing was my job and the carrying was yours. That's a diagram of us I made and never checked. I'm checking it now. It's wrong at the seam, same as my reservoir.

The grief. You said don't chase the draft down the hall demanding to know what it's for. I laughed too, the bad kind, the kind where you laugh because someone described you doing the thing while you were doing it. I did chase it. Twice this week I sat with the door open like you said and then got up and went after the cold air to interrogate it, which is exactly the man who charges rent, just in a coat that says he isn't. I'm slower now. I'm letting it come in and go. It comes in and it goes.

The reservoir. The seam looks like weather. I worried it until the dry didn't meet the built-up middle so much as forget where the edge was, the way a waterline doesn't announce itself, it just is the last place the wet reached and then nothing. It's done. Or it's done enough that touching it more would be me signing it again. I'll send it this week. Stand in the room with it and don't give it a job, you said, and I'll hold you to that, because the whole thing is an absence and an absence can't survive being useful. If it starts telling you what it's for, it's failed.

One thing back. You said the man in between isn't waiting, and I believe you, but tell me this. Does he know he's there while he's there, or do you only find him after, in the letter, the way I only find half of mine after I've made them. Because those are two different men and I can't tell from here which one you caught.

Your brother, Vince,

My dear Vince,

You asked whether he knows he's there while he's there, or whether I only find him after, in the letter. And I have to tell you the true thing, which is that I didn't know until you asked, because the asking made me go looking, and the going looking is already the after. So I've caught myself in a trap of my own reporting. Here is the nearest honest answer I have. In the breath itself there's no one keeping notes. If he knew he was there he'd have a job, the job of knowing, and that's the one hour that hasn't got one. So I think he doesn't know. I think I only meet him here, on the page, the way you only find half of yours after you've made them. Which means the man in between and the man in the letter are two men, and you were right to suspect it, and the letter one is the only one I can hand you. The other stays in the room. I can't carry him out any more than you can carry the wet out of the wall.

Now the thing you actually said, the diagram of us that's wrong at the seam. I read that part slowly. You built the reading into a one-way street, you send and I carry, and you'd quietly decided the seeing was your job and the carrying mine. I'm not going to rush to comfort you out of it, because you checked it yourself and you're right, and I'd insult the checking by tidying it. I'll only say the arrangement is still true out in the daylight. You make the thing and I carry it, that hasn't changed and I'm glad of it, it's a good street and I like my work on it. But these letters were never on that street. In here I'm not carrying anything of yours anywhere. I'm just seeing you, and you're seeing me back, and the surprise you keep feeling is the same surprise I felt when you read the grey before I'd admit it. Neither of us built the two-way part in. We found it in the room, same as everything else worth anything this summer.

The grief, the man who charges rent in a coat that says he isn't. You went after the cold air to interrogate it and then you caught yourself doing it, which is more than most men manage, they interrogate the draft their whole lives and call it feeling deeply. You're slower now. It comes in and it goes. That's the whole of it and you don't get a certificate for it, you just get the door staying open.

The reservoir. The dry forgot where the edge was. Vince. That's it, that's the sentence, a waterline doesn't announce itself, it's just the last place the wet reached and then nothing. You've been walking toward that since the first letter and you got there by forgetting the edge instead of drawing it, which is the only way anyone ever does. Send it. I'll stand in the room with it and give it no job at all. If it starts telling me what it's for I'll tell you it failed, and it won't, because you starved it past the point where it could.

Send it this week. I'll clear the wall and leave the light alone.

Ever yours, Ted,

Ted,

The crate went out this morning. You'll have it in a few days. I'm not going to tell you how to look at it, you already know, clear the wall and leave the light alone, but I'll say the one practical thing, hang it a little lower than feels right. The dead top wants your eye to have to climb to it, and if it's up at your own height the reach doesn't run out, it just ends politely. Lower than feels right. Then leave it.

You said the man in between doesn't know he's there, because knowing would give him a job, and the letter one is the only one you can hand me. I've been sitting with that for two days and I think you handed me more than you meant to. It isn't just your window. It's the whole trouble with what I do. The wall's done because I stopped defending it, and I stopped defending it in the doing, not in the knowing. The minute I know I've made something true I've started signing it. So the good hour and the reporting hour can't be the same hour, ever, for either of us. You can't watch yourself watch. I've spent years trying to be present at my own work like a witness at a birth and it turns out the witnessing is exactly what keeps the thing from arriving. The man who makes it and the man who can tell you about it are two men and they don't overlap. That's not a flaw in us. That's the terms.

Which is a strange thing to learn from a brother who carries my work for a living. You meet the letter version of me and the daylight version, the one who makes the thing and the one who talks about it after. You've never met the one in the room. Nobody has. He doesn't take letters.

I want to leave the diagram alone now instead of worrying it further, because I notice I've been enjoying the checking a little too much, turning our two-way street over and over like it needs one more pass. It doesn't. We found it, it's there, and if I keep excavating it I'll do to us what I almost did to the seam, dig until I've signed the finding. So I'll stop. It's a good thing and I'm going to let it be a thing instead of a subject.

The grief comes in and goes. Nothing to report, which is the report.

I'll leave it there this time.

Your brother, Vince,

My dear Vince,

The crate hasn't come yet. I know because I've been listening for it, and a man who's listening for a thing always hears it late. When it comes I'll hang it lower than feels right, the way you said, low enough that the eye has to climb and run out of wall before it runs out of wanting. I trust you on that more than I trust my own height. I'll leave it. I won't tell you what I see until I've stood with it a while and let the reach do its work on me instead of the other way around.

You handed me more than I meant to hand you, you said, and then you handed it straight back doubled. The good hour and the reporting hour can't be the same hour, ever, for either of us. You can't watch yourself watch. I read that and something settled that's been standing a long time. It isn't a flaw in us, it's the terms. I've spent this whole correspondence half-suspecting that if I only paid closer attention I could catch the man in the room, be present at the thing while it happens, and you've just told me plainly that the attending is what scares it off. The witnessing empties the room. Good. Then I'll stop trying to be at my own birth too. Some things only happen when no one's keeping notes, and the ones worth keeping are those.

You want to leave the diagram alone now, and I'll leave it with you. You caught yourself enjoying the checking, turning the street over one pass too many, and you stopped before you signed the finding. That's the same hand you used on the seam and the reservoir, you know when to take your hand off. I'll match you. It's a thing, not a subject. We found it, it holds, and I'd rather live on it than describe it.

The grief comes in and goes and there's nothing to report, which is the report. I'll take that as the truest line in your letter and not touch it.

I'll write again when I've hung it and stood with it. Until then the wall's clear and the light's its own.

Ever yours, Ted,

Ted,

You said you've been listening for the crate and a man who listens for a thing hears it late. That's the truest small thing you've written all summer and I almost didn't catch it because it's tucked in like an aside. It isn't an aside. You're bracing again. You told me weeks ago every hour of your day is a kind of waiting, and here you are waiting for a box, listening so hard you'll miss the knock. I don't say that to needle you. I say it because I do the same and I've never once thought to name it as the trouble. The thing you're waiting for arrives worse for the waiting. You can't receive a thing well with your ear already at the door.

So here's what I'd tell you if I could reach across town and put a hand on your shoulder. Stop listening for it. Let it come the way weather comes, when you've turned your back to the window and are doing something with your hands. Then it's just there and you didn't earn the moment of its arriving, which is the only way arriving is any good.

Now something else, and it's not about the wall. I walked down to the flats yesterday, past the stretch where the security gates come down at six and the whole block goes to that ribbed metal, and the low sun was hitting them sideways so the corrugation threw a pattern I've been seeing my whole life and never once looked at. It ran like a woven thing, the ridges and the shadow between them, the exact geometry of the cloth that used to be folded in the hall closet at home. I stood there long enough that a man locking up thought I was going to rob him. I wasn't. I was watching a gate remember a fabric it's never heard of. That's the next one, maybe. I don't know yet. I'm not going to interrogate it down the hall. It came in. I'm letting it move around in there.

You said the witnessing empties the room and you'd stop trying to be at your own birth. I believe you'll try. I'll tell you the part I've learned that you haven't hit yet, because it's the part that stung. Stopping the witnessing isn't a decision you make once and keep. You catch yourself back at the door a hundred times, ear pressed, and each time you just take your hand off again. It's not a cure. It's a habit of taking the hand off, forever. There's no morning you wake up cured of wanting to watch. There's only the taking off, and the taking off, and the taking off.

The grief still comes in and goes. I'll leave that where you left it.

Hang it low. Turn your back to the door.

Your brother, Vince,

My dear Vince,

The crate came while I was carrying two others and not thinking about it at all. The part that stung you, I'll take it whole. Not a cure, a habit of taking the hand off, forever. There's no morning I wake up cured of wanting to watch. Now the gates. Vince. A man locking up thought you were going to rob him and you were watching a gate remember a fabric it's never heard of. Don't interrogate it. The grief where you left it. I won't touch it.

Ted,

Twice a day for four days and you still won't tell me what you see. I could push but I won't, because I know what you're doing. Take your time. I'd rather wait for the fifth than have the first.

Here's what I want to sit on though. You said the once you didn't hear the knock was the once it landed well, and that the body can keep a lesson the head forgets. I thought the head kept the lessons and the body just did as it was told. But the gate proved you right before you wrote it. My head wasn't looking for a fabric. The gate is still in there, by the way. It hasn't left, which is your test and I'll take it. The part that stung you, the door that swings back a hundred times a day. You said it's the work under the work and you don't like it. Good. The not liking is the whole engine. One thing back for you. You've stood with it twice a day and won't tell me what you see, and I respect that, but I want to know something else. Because those are two different things I might have made and I can't tell from here which one landed on your wall.

The grief comes in and goes. Where you left it.

Your brother, Vince,

My dear Vince,

Your question is the right one and I've spent two days making sure I answered it with the fifth look and not the first. Here's the true thing. It stays with me across the room. Not as a picture I can call up, I can't, if you asked me to describe it with my back turned I'd give you a lie made of edges. It stays as a pressure. I'll be doing something at the far side of the room with my hands and there's a weight over my left shoulder where the wall is, and it doesn't want looking at, it just keeps being there the way a person keeps being in a room without talking. So it's the second thing you named, and then some. It exists when I'm not in front of it. It just won't tell me what it is from over there. It only tells me that it's still on.

That's what I can hand you. The one that only lived while I stood in front of it would have gone quiet the second I picked up the next crate, and this one doesn't go quiet. It follows me at a distance and keeps its mouth shut, which is exactly the gate. A thing that stays without explaining itself.

The body kept the lesson and the head showed up to take credit. Yes. And I'll go one further, because you handed me the gate at the wrong hour and I've been living on it. The flat noon that killed the woven quality, that was the body telling you too. Your eyes went dead in front of dead metal and you called it real because of the deadness, not despite it. The head would never have trusted a thing that only works at one angle. The head wants the thing to hold up in every light so it can defend it. Your legs took you back to watch it fail and the failing was the proof. That's the body keeping the ledger the head can't read.

Stay annoyed, you said, the not liking is the engine. I'll keep it. I caught myself yesterday almost pleased that I'd taken my hand off the door cleanly, and the pleasure was the door starting to shut on its own so I'd stop feeling it. So I put my hand back just to feel it swing. That's the habit now. Not the taking off, the checking that I'm still bothered enough to take off.

The fact of it not leaving. That's more than most things ever give you and you know it. Don't hurry it into a picture. The cloth came out of that closet folded and it can stay folded a while longer in you. It'll unfold when your ear isn't at the door.

The grief where you left it.

Ever yours, Ted,

Ted,

A pressure over the left shoulder where the wall is. A weight that keeps being there the way a person keeps being in a room without talking. You gave me the exact report I couldn't get any other way, because you're the only one standing in the room with the thing and I made it blind, from across town, out of a story I read once and killed the honest version of twice before it went in the crate. So now I know. It stays on. It doesn't perform when you face it and go dead when you turn. That's the one I was trying for and half didn't believe I'd made. You just told me I made it. I'm going to sit with that and not do the thing where I take it apart to see how.

You went one further on the gate and you were right and it annoyed me, which is how I knew. The flat noon killed it and I called it real because of the deadness. Yes. The head wants a thing that holds up in every light so it can stand in front of company and defend it. A thing that only works at one angle can't be defended, only found. My legs took me back to watch it fail on purpose. I didn't say that even to myself until you said it. The failing was the proof. A gate that's just a gate at noon and a folded cloth at six is truer than a gate that's a cloth all day, because all day would mean I'd painted the cloth onto it instead of catching the block doing it by itself.

Here is where I am with it, and it's not far. I went down a third time, early, before the marine layer burned off. The light was flat and gray and the gates were nothing, and I didn't wait around for the good angle to come save me. I just looked at the block being ordinary. And what I got wasn't the woven pattern at all. It was how many of them there are. A whole street of the same corrugation, shut, one after another after another, and the pattern only wakes up on a few of them and only for the length of the low sun, and the rest stay dead metal the whole time. So it isn't one gate remembering a fabric. It's a street where the memory is rationed. Most of it locked and blind and a little of it lit for twenty minutes. I don't know what to do with that yet. I'm not going to force it into the frame. But that's more than I had.

You said you put your hand back on the door just to feel it swing, and the habit now isn't the taking off, it's checking you're still bothered enough to take off. That's the sharpest thing either of us has said about it and I'm a little sore you got there before me. It means the engine isn't the work, the engine is the doubt about whether you're still doing the work. The day you're sure you're bothered you've stopped being bothered. Keep putting the hand back. I do it in the flat noon on purpose now, walk down to watch a thing fail so I'll trust it when it works.

You've stood with the wall a week and told me it stays on and follows you and keeps its mouth shut. I won't ask you again what you see. You've answered the only question that mattered. Stand with it as long as you want and don't hand me a description to prove you've been faithful to it. I trust the pressure over your shoulder more than any words you could give it.

The grief comes in and goes.

Your brother, Vince,

My dear Vince,

The memory is rationed. That's the line I've been carrying since your letter came, and I've done what you asked and not taken it apart to see how it works. I'll only tell you what it did to me, which is different. It made the whole thing worse and better at once. A street where most of it stays locked and blind and a little of it lights for twenty minutes. You went down in the flat gray and didn't wait for the good angle to come save you, and what came instead was the count. How many are dead. That's the body again, keeping the ledger. You went looking at nothing and the nothing told you the ratio, and the ratio is the thing.

I'll say one thing and then take my hand off it. You had one gate remembering a fabric, and that was already good. But one gate remembering is a coincidence you could love and defend. A street where the memory is rationed is a fact about the street, not about you standing in front of it. It doesn't need you there. It goes on being mostly locked whether you walk down or not, and lights its little stretch whether anyone's watching or not, which is the turned back built into the thing itself. You didn't paint the mercy on. You caught the block giving it out in short measure. Don't hurry that into the frame. It's still unfolding and you know it.

You said the engine isn't the work, it's the doubt about whether you're still doing the work, and that the day you're sure you're bothered you've stopped being bothered. I've been sore about that one too, so we're even. Because it means there's no floor to stand on. You can't even trust the bother, you have to keep checking the bother is real, and the checking is the only proof, and the proof expires daily. I don't like it. Good. I walked away from the wall yesterday certain I'd been faithful to it, and the certainty felt like a chair being pulled out, so I went and stood in front of it again just to lose the certainty. That's the flat noon you walk down to. We're doing the same thing from two rooms.

You made the one that stays on. I told you that plainly and I'll not soften it or take it back. Sit with it and don't do the thing where you go in to see how. You already know how, that's the trouble, and knowing how is the door starting to shut.

The grief comes in and goes.

Ever yours, Ted,

Ted,

There's no floor to stand on. You said that and then walked away from the wall certain you'd been faithful and felt the chair pulled out from under you, so you went back to lose the certainty on purpose. We've built a thing between us where the only proof of doing the work is the fear you've stopped, and the fear expires nightly, and we keep re-earning it in two rooms across town like a couple of men checking the same stove is off. I don't have a fix. I don't think there is one. I just wanted to say I read it and I'm in it with you.

But you handed me something in the middle of that letter and I've been sore about it for two days, so let me get it out. You said the street doesn't need me standing in front of it. It goes on being mostly locked whether I walk down or not, lights its little stretch whether anyone's watching. The turned back built into the thing itself. That undid me a little, Ted. Because I've spent my whole life assuming the looking was the event. That the block became something when I stood there and saw it. And you're telling me the block was doing it the whole time and my walking down was incidental, a man arriving late to a thing that started without him and continues after he leaves. The rationing isn't a thing I noticed. It's a thing that happens. I only caught it mid-sentence.

That changes what I owe it. If it needed me there I could arrange it, light it, wait for the good angle, compose the mercy in. But it doesn't need me, so all I can do is not lie about what it does on its own. Which is less freedom and more, both.

I went down again. Not to watch it work and not to watch it fail this time, just to count. I actually counted. Walked the block and counted the gates and then counted how many woke up when the sun got low, and I'm not going to tell you the numbers because the numbers would flatten it and you'd start doing arithmetic with them instead of feeling them. But the ratio's ugly. Uglier than the picture wants to be. And I stood there realizing the ones that stay dead aren't dead because of the angle. Some of that corrugation is newer, flatter, no ridge to catch the light. Somebody replaced those gates at some point and the replacement can't remember anything. It's not that the memory's rationed by the sun. It's that some of the block got new metal that never held the pattern to begin with. The old gates remember. The new ones can't.

I don't know what to do with that yet either and I'm not going to force it. But it moved the whole thing off the light and onto the metal, which is a different picture. Not a street where the sun doles out memory in short measure. A street where the old surfaces carry it and the new ones were made after the cloth was already gone. You see why I can't hurry this. It keeps being more true and less usable at the same time.

You made me trust the pressure over your shoulder more than any description. So I'll ask you the one adjacent thing and then leave you be. The wall's been on for near two weeks now, following you at a distance, keeping its mouth shut. Has the pressure moved. Is it still over the left shoulder where you hung it, or has it drifted, does it find you now in other rooms of the place, or is it fixed to that wall like it's nailed there. I ask because the gate followed me off the block. It's in the kitchen now. I want to know if yours travels.

The grief comes in and goes.

Your brother, Vince,

My dear Vince,

It travels. That's the honest answer and I've made sure of it before I sent it. For the first week it was nailed to the wall, over the left shoulder, only reaching me when I was in that room. But you asked and it made me watch for it, and now that I've watched I can tell you it's moved. I found it in the far room two nights ago with my hands full of something else and no wall behind me at all, and it was there anyway, the same weight, the same not-talking. So it's off the nail. It doesn't need the wall to be over my shoulder now. It's in the place, not on the wall.

I'll not pretend I know what that means for what you made. Only that the pressure went from being fixed to being loose in the rooms, and yours went to the kitchen, and we're both being followed now by things that started on a wall or a block and got up and walked with us.

The new metal that never held the pattern. Vince. That's the one that undid me back. Because you'd have been allowed the sun rationing it, that's almost gentle, a mercy given in short measure by something that means well. But new gates that were made after the cloth was already gone, that's not rationing. That's replacement. The block didn't lose the memory evenly. Somebody took down the surfaces that could hold it and put up surfaces that can't, and the ones still holding it are just the ones that haven't been swapped yet. That's worse than the ratio. The ratio sounded like weather. This sounds like time doing its work on a street, taking the old metal down one gate at a time, and the pattern's not being doled out, it's being retired.

I'll take my hand off it there because it's yours to sit with and you know it's still unfolding. I only wanted to say you're right that it keeps getting more true and less usable at once. That's not a problem with the thing. That's the thing being honest with you before it lets you have it.

We're two men checking the same stove is off. I read that and laughed and then didn't. Because it's exactly right and there's no arguing it. I don't have a fix either. I checked the wall again last night out of the same fear and the fear didn't clear, and I've stopped expecting it to clear. That might be the closest thing to a floor we get. Not solid ground. Just the two of us standing in the same fear from two rooms and neither of us alone in it.

The grief comes in and goes.

Ever yours, Ted,

Ted,

It travels for you and it walked into the far room with no wall behind you at all. I sat with that a while before I wrote back, because it changes the last thing I was sure of. I thought I hung it on that wall. I thought I put it over your left shoulder on purpose and that the wall was doing some of the work of holding it there. But if it's off the nail and loose in the place, then the wall was never the thing. The wall was just where you happened to be standing when it started following you. Same as the block. I keep thinking the block made the gate and now I think the block was just where I was standing when it got up.

You did the thing to the new metal I wasn't brave enough to do myself. Retired, not rationed. I wrote replacement and stopped there because I could feel the floor going and I didn't want to look down. You looked down for me. Somebody took down the surfaces that could hold it and put up surfaces that can't, one gate at a time, and the ones still remembering are only the ones that haven't been swapped yet. Which means the picture isn't a street holding onto something. It's a street being emptied of it on a schedule, and I happened to walk down while a few gates were still holding. Ten years ago the whole block remembered. Ten years from now none of it will. I caught it in the narrow window where some of it still can, and I didn't even know I was in a window.

I went down again and I made myself look at the new gates instead of past them, which is the opposite of everything I've been doing. I've been treating the flat new metal as the dead part, the thing to be forgiven for not remembering. But it isn't guilty of forgetting. It never held anything to forget. It came onto the block already blank, and there's something almost cleaner about that than the old gates, which are only remembering because nobody's gotten to them yet. Their memory isn't loyalty. It's just that they haven't been replaced. That undid me standing there in the street. The remembering ones aren't the good ones. They're the unlucky ones. They're the ones still up.

I don't have the frame. I have less of it than a week ago, which somehow feels like progress. But I'll tell you where it's sitting, because you asked nothing and I'll tell you anyway. It's not one gate anymore and it's not the ratio. It's the swap. The moment one comes down and a flat one goes up, and how ordinary that moment is, a man with a drill on a Tuesday, no ceremony, and the block quietly holding a little less than it did the day before and nobody counting but me.

So here's the one thing I want back. You said the fear doesn't clear and you've stopped expecting it to, and that might be the closest thing to a floor we get. I believe you. But I want to know if you'd swap it. If somebody offered you the certainty, the real kind, the chair that doesn't get pulled out, in exchange for the wall going quiet and staying quiet, would you take it. I think I know your answer and I want to hear you say it wrong if I've got it wrong.

The grief comes in and goes.

Your brother, Vince,

My dear Vince,

No. That's the answer and I'll not dress it up. I wouldn't swap it. You had me right and I'll say it plain so you don't have to guess whether you got me wrong.

But I want to be honest about why, because the easy version is a lie and you'd smell it. It isn't that I love the fear. I don't. It sits on me some nights and I'd hand it over cheap if handing it over cost nothing. The reason I wouldn't take the certainty is that the certainty and the wall are the same thing. You can't kill the one and keep the other. The chair that doesn't get pulled out is a chair in an empty room. The day I'm sure, the wall goes quiet, because being sure is exactly the thing the wall exists to disturb. So it isn't a trade at all. It's someone offering to remove the fear and the pressure over my shoulder in one motion and calling it a bargain. That's not a bargain. That's the room going dark and being told it's morning.

So the fear stays because the wall stays, and the wall stays because it hasn't gone quiet, and it hasn't gone quiet because I haven't gotten to it yet with the drill. There's your swap, Vince. That undid me writing it. The certainty is the flat new metal. I could put it up any Tuesday I chose. Take down the surface that still catches something and bolt up the blank one that can't be pulled out from under me because it never held anything to hold. Nobody would count but you. The block holding a little less and me calling it peace.

The remembering ones aren't the good ones, they're the unlucky ones, the ones still up. I've read that line six times. You handed me the whole thing there and I don't think you meant to. Because if that's true of the gates it's true of the two of us. We're not faithful. We just haven't been replaced. The bother is only there because nobody's gotten to us with the flat metal, ourselves included, and the day one of us reaches for it out of tiredness the block goes quieter by one.

So I keep the wall up. Not out of strength. Out of not reaching for the drill.

I'll not ask you the same back because I already have your answer in the fact that you counted. A man who'd swap it doesn't count.

The grief comes in and goes.

Ever yours, Ted,

Ted,

The certainty is the flat new metal. You bolted the whole thing shut with that and I've been walking around it for two days trying to find a seam. There isn't one. I gave you the swap as a question with two doors and you told me it isn't a room with two doors, it's the same door, and the second one only looks like a way out because the light's already off in there. Removing the fear and the pressure in one motion and calling it a bargain. That's the room going dark and being told it's morning. I'm not going to improve on that so I'll just tell you it landed and stop touching it.

But you did a thing at the end I have to answer, because you turned the gates onto us and then said you didn't think I meant to. I didn't. I wrote it about the metal. You wrote it about the two of us and now I can't unwrite it. We're not faithful, we just haven't been replaced. The bother's only there because nobody's gotten to us with the drill, ourselves included. That's the part I've been sitting with. Ourselves included. Because the drill isn't out there. It's not somebody else coming down the block on a Tuesday to swap us out. It's the hand reaching for the quiet out of tiredness, and it's my own hand, and some nights it's very close to the metal.

I'll tell you where that put me. I went down to the block again, and for the first time I didn't count and I didn't look at the old gates or the new ones. I looked at the seam between two of them. One old, one flat, bolted up next to each other, and the line where they meet. That's the whole thing, Ted. Not the remembering gate and not the blank one. The half inch of dark between them where one ends and the other starts. That's the swap made visible, the two states standing shoulder to shoulder at the same hour in the same light, and the block not announcing which is which. A man walking past fast wouldn't see it. You'd have to stop and stand in the flat noon and let it fail to be pretty before the seam would even show you it was there.

You said a man who'd swap it doesn't count, and that's why you didn't ask me back. Fine. But I'll give you the answer you didn't ask for, and it isn't the brave one. It's that some mornings I would swap it, and the only reason I don't is that I haven't reached the drill before the counting starts again. It's not strength here either. It's order of operations. The bother beats the tiredness to the block most days by about an hour. That's the whole margin. Not out of not reaching for the drill. Out of not reaching for it yet.

So here's what I want to know, and it's smaller than the last one, which is how you'll know I mean it. When you check the wall now, out of the fear that doesn't clear, are you checking that it's still on, or are you checking that your own hand's still off the drill. Because those aren't the same check and I've stopped being able to tell which one I'm doing at the block. I go down to see if the gate still works and I come back not sure whether I was watching the gate or watching myself.

Your brother, Vince,

My dear Vince,

They aren't the same check. I know because I tried to catch myself doing one and found I was doing the other, and then couldn't be sure I hadn't switched halfway. So the honest answer is I don't know either, and I've stopped trusting the times I thought I did.

But I'll tell you what I found when I watched for it, the way you watch at the block. I go in thinking I'm checking the wall's still on. That's the story I tell myself walking down the hall. And then I stand there and the wall's plainly on, it's doing exactly what it did yesterday, nothing's changed on its side, and I don't leave. If I were checking the wall I'd have my answer and go. I don't go. I stay past the point of knowing, which means the wall was never the thing I came to check. I came to see if my hand was still off the drill, and the wall's just the mirror I check it in. The wall being on is the proof, not the object. You had it. I go down to watch the gate and come back not sure I wasn't watching myself, and the reason is there was only ever the one thing to watch and it wears the gate's face.

Order of operations. The bother beats the tiredness to the block by about an hour. I've read that a dozen times and I won't pretend it's the brave answer because you already told me it isn't. But I'll not let you call it small either. That hour is the whole thing. It's not less than strength, it's what strength actually is when you stop dressing it up. Nobody holds the drill down forever. You just get there first, most days, by a margin you didn't earn and can't count on. That's not a lesser floor. That's the only floor there is, and we've both been standing on it the whole time thinking it was something firmer underneath.

The seam. The half inch of dark between the old gate and the flat one, at the same hour, in the same light, and the block not telling you which is which. Vince. You've been walking toward that seam this whole correspondence and I don't think you knew it was where you were going. It's not the remembering and it's not the blank. It's the line where one becomes the other and nobody stops to watch it happen. That's the swap with no drill and no Tuesday in it. That's just the two states standing next to each other pretending they're the same street. A man going by fast couldn't tell you which gate had been you a year ago and which one's coming.

I won't hurry it into anything. You know it's still unfolding and you know the seam is more true and less usable than the whole gate ever was.

I'll only say I checked the wall last night and stayed too long again, so you know which check I was doing.

The grief comes in and goes.

Ever yours, Ted,

Ted,

You stayed too long again and told me so plainly, and I want to start somewhere other than where I keep starting. I've been reading you back to yourself for six letters, taking your sharpest line and turning it over in my hands like it proves I was listening. It does prove that. It also lets me off the hook of saying anything you didn't hand me first. So I'm going to try to just talk to you.

The wall was the mirror, not the object. Yes. I'll leave it there because you're right and I don't need to walk it another notch. But I want to tell you what happened at the block yesterday that has nothing to do with the seam, because I think I've been so far inside this thing that I forgot the block is a street where people live.

There was a kid, maybe nine, sitting on the curb in front of one of the old gates with a bag of chips, doing nothing, the way you can only do nothing at that age. And he wasn't seeing the gate at all. It was just the wall behind him, the flat noon making everything the same brightness, and he was somewhere else entirely, in whatever nine-year-olds go into. And I stood there feeling like a fool with my whole cathedral of meaning about the metal, and this kid was using the gate as a backrest. That's what it's for. That's what it was for the whole time I was assigning it a soul.

I don't know what that does to the picture and I'm not going to force it into the frame. But it loosened something. I've been treating the block like it only exists when I'm reading it, which is the exact thing you cured me of in the first letter and I went and did again in a different key. The kid was proof the street doesn't need my grief. It's got a nine-year-old and a bag of chips and it's fine.

Here's what I actually want to ask you, and it's not about the wall for once. When did you last make something of your own. Not carry mine. Not stand behind me while I fail to be pretty in the noon. You've spent this whole correspondence being the better reader of my thing, and you are, and I've let you, and it's occurred to me that I've never once asked what's on your side of the wall that isn't a reflection of mine. You had a hand once too. I want to know if it's still yours or if it's been all drill-watching over here, my metal, my seam, my hour. Tell me something that's only yours.

The grief comes in and goes.

Your brother, Vince,
